# Agent SDK full documentation

> Build and serve bots and agents from versioned Markdown and TypeScript.

---

Source: /docs/building-with-agents.md

# Build with a coding agent

A coding agent in your checkout can create an Agent SDK project, call its tools, run a real turn, and check the result from the CLI. You approve the plan and any side effects.

To let a running agent change its own source, see the [self-improvement extension](/docs/guides/improve.md).

## Create an agent from a goal

Tell the coding agent what the agent is for and where people reach it, and ask it to follow the `bdk-create-agent` skill. It asks for any decisions you haven't made, shows a file plan, and scaffolds a small first version with a smoke eval.

## Add one capability

For an existing project, name the outcome and point the coding agent at the matching skill, such as `bdk-setup-slack`, `bdk-mcp-auth`, or `bdk-github`. For example:

> Add Slack mentions and DMs to this agent. Follow the bdk-setup-slack
> skill, keep replies in the source thread, and verify one local mention.

> Connect the private inventory MCP server with host OAuth. Keep its
> write tools behind a narrow server-tool wrapper.

> Add a GitHub ready-for-review trigger and replay PR 42 before posting
> anything live.

## Verify tools before tuning the prompt

Have the coding agent call tools directly and fix any that return the wrong evidence before it touches the instructions. Then it runs one real turn, reads the trace that `run` prints, and runs the smoke evals:

```bash
agent-sdk validate --dir .
agent-sdk info --dir . --json
agent-sdk tool call inspect_pr --dir . --input '{"prUrl":"https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42"}'
agent-sdk run --dir . --message "Is https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42 ready to approve?"
agent-sdk session get --file <trace-path-printed-by-run>
agent-sdk eval --dir . --tag smoke
```

Finish with the project's TypeScript check, because a passing turn doesn't prove the project type-checks. Only `run` and `eval` need a Cursor credential, and [Environment variables](/docs/reference/cli.md#environment-variables) lists the ways to provide one.

## Improve a working agent

Once a smoke turn passes, follow [Hillclimbing](/docs/hillclimbing.md) to improve the agent against fixed inputs.

# Deploy an Agent SDK project

Deploy a pushed Git ref as a stable service on Cursor-managed hosting, or
self-host it when you need your own network or process controls.

## Deploy from Git

Commit and push the ref you want to run, then deploy it:

```bash
cd my-agent
agent-sdk login
agent-sdk validate
agent-sdk deploy
```

The command waits until the agent is running and prints its URL. Open [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents) to see the agent and manage it.

`deploy` builds the pushed ref, so uncommitted changes don't ship. Pass the source when the checkout is not the one you want:

```text
agent-sdk deploy \
  --repo https://github.com/acme/agents \
  --ref main \
  --path agents/weather \
  --slug weather-agent
```

### Connect deployed peers

To call another agent your team deployed, add
`defineConnection({ agent: "weather-agent" })` to the caller and redeploy
it. See [Peer agents](/docs/guides/agent-to-agent.md).

### Privacy Mode

Managed hosting stores your repository and the agent's data, so it depends
on your privacy setting:

| Privacy setting | Managed hosting |
| --- | --- |
| Privacy Mode | Available. Cursor stores deployment data the same way it does without Privacy Mode, and the agent's model requests get the same Privacy Mode handling as your other Cursor requests. |
| Privacy Mode (Legacy) | Not available. `deploy`, a hosted session, and an eval run all refuse. |

Switch to Privacy Mode, or ask a team admin when your team enforces the
setting.

## Add egress and secrets

Declare the hosts and secret names your code calls. `agent-sdk info --dir .`
shows them combined with what mounted extensions add.

```ts
// bot/agent.ts
import { defineAgent } from "@grok/agent-sdk";

export default defineAgent({
  hosting: {
    egressDomains: ["api.weather.example.com"],
    secretNames: ["WEATHER_API_KEY"],
  },
});
```

After you deploy, set each value at the hidden prompt. The next task uses
the new value without another deploy.

```bash
agent-sdk secret set weather-agent WEATHER_API_KEY
agent-sdk secret list weather-agent
```

Commit secret names, never values. Don't pass `NAME=VALUE` to `secret set`
or use a name that starts with `CURSOR_`.

Hosted secrets arrive after your modules load, so read each one inside the
handler, tool, or callback that needs it. Give an MCP connection a
[`${NAME}` template](/docs/reference/connections.md#credentials-in-headers-and-env)
instead.

SCM channels take each credential as a named secret, such as
`{ secretName: "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }`. The channel reads the environment
variable with that name locally and the deployment secret on Cursor hosting.
On Cursor hosting, Cursor rejects a badly signed delivery before it reaches your agent. `validate`
fails on a literal or a getter.

Write each egress host as a lowercase hostname with no scheme or path, such as `api.example.com`, and add a port such as `clickhouse.example.com:9440` only for raw TCP. `agent-sdk deploy` rejects any other form, and the error quotes that host.

Your team's egress policy limits which hosts you can list in
`hosting.egressDomains`. If you list a host that the policy blocks,
`agent-sdk deploy` fails and the error names that host. A deployment that
is already running keeps the policy from its last successful deploy. Ask a
team admin to add the host, or remove it and deploy again.

| Team egress mode | What `agent-sdk deploy` allows |
| --- | --- |
| No mode set | Every host in `hosting.egressDomains`. |
| Allow all network access | Every host in `hosting.egressDomains`. The bot stays limited to that list. |
| Defaults + team allowlist | The platform default list, plus the team list. |
| Team allowlist only | The team list. |

No team list can remove the platform base, which includes Cursor's API and
the npm registry. `agent-sdk deploy --json` lists every allowed host under
`egress.effective`.

A team entry `*.example.com` allows `example.com`, every subdomain, and
narrower wildcards such as `*.api.example.com`. An agent entry
`*.example.com` skips the apex, so list `example.com` too when the agent
calls it.

A raw TCP host such as `db.example.com:5432` needs a team `CIDR:port` entry
that covers every public IPv4 address it resolves to. If your team
restricts egress, a PlanetScale Postgres host (`*.pg.psdb.cloud`) needs a
team `CIDR:port` entry for ports 5432 and 6432.

## Use the hosted agent

### Verify a hosted turn

```bash
agent-sdk session create --slug weather-agent --message "Forecast for Paris" --wait
agent-sdk session get ses_... --prod --slug weather-agent
agent-sdk session get ses_... --prod --slug weather-agent --view events
agent-sdk logs --prod --slug weather-agent
```

Without `--wait`, the command returns before the session exists, so the
output has no `sessionId` yet. A long turn can show `running` with no logs
for several minutes. If the event count keeps going up, the turn is still
working.

### Send work to the deployment

Call a custom route on the stable alias URL with the alias token:

```bash
curl -X POST "$AGENT_ALIAS_URL/v1/channels/tickets/ticket" \
  -H "X-Agent-Alias-Token: $AGENT_ALIAS_TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ticketId":"ENG-142","message":"CSV export returns 500"}'
```

See [Route responses](/docs/reference/channels.md#route-responses) for what the
caller gets back. To confirm the work started, run
`agent-sdk session list --prod --slug weather-agent`.

### Protect the alias token

The first deploy prints the alias token once. If it leaks or you lose it, run `agent-sdk deployment rotate-token weather-agent`. Output from `deployment --json` can include access headers, so guard it the same way.

Use [`publicEndpoint()`](/docs/guides/webhooks.md) only for a webhook provider
that can't send the token and whose signature the channel verifies.

## Update the deployment

Push the new ref and deploy the same slug. Each redeploy replaces the
watched repositories, so pass every `--cursor-events-repo` value again, or
the deployment watches only its GitHub source repository. Run
`agent-sdk deployment get weather-agent` to check a rollout.

## Keep state across replacements

Sessions, `ctx.host.kv`, and `ctx.host.files` survive restarts and
redeploys. Anything else the agent writes to disk can disappear.

## Self-host securely

Run Agent SDK under Node 22.13 or newer, never Bun. One process can serve
every agent under a directory:

```bash
export CURSOR_API_KEY="<cursor-api-key>"
export AGENT_SDK_BEARER_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"

agent-sdk serve \
  --dir /srv/agents \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 3000 \
  --state-root /var/lib/agent-sdk \
  --bearer-token "$AGENT_SDK_BEARER_TOKEN"
```

Before you expose the host:

- Put TLS or an authenticating proxy in front of the server.
- Keep `--bearer-token` unless a proxy authenticates every caller.
- Keep `--state-root` on a backed-up persistent volume outside the
  repository.
- Turn on schedules in only one process per project.

In a container, use `--host 0.0.0.0` behind an authenticating network
boundary.

Source: /docs/evals.md

# Evals

An eval sends a fixed input to the real agent and checks which tools ran and what the answer looks
like. To improve an agent and lock each win with an eval, follow [Hillclimbing](/docs/hillclimbing.md).

Evals run real tools, so [guard any writes](#keep-side-effects-out-of-eval-sessions) first.

## Protect a tool decision

The case below passes only if the agent calls the inspection tool and doesn't approve.

```ts
// evals/readiness.eval.ts
import { defineEval, includes } from "@grok/agent-sdk/evals";

export default defineEval({
  tags: ["smoke"],
  async test(t) {
    await t.send("Is https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42 ready to approve?");

    t.succeeded();
    t.calledTool("inspect_pr");
    t.notCalledTool("approve_pr");
    t.check(t.reply, includes(/ready|blocked|approve/i));
  },
});
```

Evals live in `evals/` beside `bot/`. Set how many cases run at once:

```ts
// evals/evals.config.ts
import { defineEvalConfig } from "@grok/agent-sdk/evals";

export default defineEvalConfig({
  maxConcurrency: 20,
});
```

```bash
agent-sdk eval --dir . --list
agent-sdk eval --dir . --tag smoke
```

## Check answer shape or quality

When the output has a contract, check its shape:

```ts
import { matches } from "@grok/agent-sdk/evals";
import { z } from "zod";

const verdict = JSON.parse(t.reply ?? "{}");
t.check(verdict, matches(z.object({ ready: z.boolean(), blockers: z.array(z.string()) })));
```

When correctness depends on meaning, use a judge. [Judges](/docs/reference/evals.md#judges) covers
models and grader options.

```ts
t.judge.factuality("The lint step failed on src/sidebar.ts.").atLeast(0.8);
```

## Test a conversation

Several `t.send` calls in one case share a session. An assertion on a returned turn checks only that
turn, and an assertion on `t` checks the whole conversation.

```ts
const first = await t.send("Inspect PR 42.");
first.calledTool("inspect_pr");

const followUp = await t.send("Now summarize only the blockers.");
followUp.usedNoTools();
t.check(followUp.message, includes(/blocker/i));
t.succeeded();
```

## Pin realistic inputs

Seed the files the agent reads instead of depending on your checkout:

```ts
await t.send("Review pr/diff.patch and report blockers.", {
  workspaceFiles: {
    "pr/diff.patch": [
      "diff --git a/app/routes/search.ts b/app/routes/search.ts",
      "+res.send(`<h1>Results for ${req.query.q}</h1>`);",
    ].join("\n"),
  },
});
```

Save a GitHub pull request's webhook payloads as fixtures:

```bash
agent-sdk github replay https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42 \
  --events '*' --dry-run --fixtures-dir fixtures/github
```

[Datasets and fixtures](/docs/reference/evals.md#datasets-and-fixtures) covers loaders for larger sets.

## Run and debug a regression suite

Run one case while you iterate, then the smoke set before review:

```bash
agent-sdk eval --dir . readiness
agent-sdk eval --dir . --tag smoke
```

Each run writes a folder under `evals/` in the project state directory, or under `--artifacts <dir>`
if you pass it. Open `evals/<case-id>.json` in that folder to see a failed case's input, assertions,
tool calls, and final text. Model turns need a
[Cursor credential](/docs/reference/cli.md#environment-variables).

## Run evals in CI

```bash
# CURSOR_API_KEY comes from the CI secret store.
agent-sdk eval --dir . --json --no-stream \
  --junit reports/evals.xml \
  --artifacts reports/evals \
  > reports/evals.json
```

Run `--tag smoke` on pull requests and the full suite on a schedule. The
[CLI reference](/docs/reference/cli.md#eval) covers every flag.

## Keep side effects out of eval sessions

Eval sessions carry `purpose: "eval"`. Check it where the tool writes, and return the decision
without the external action:

```ts
async execute({ findings }, ctx) {
  if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
    return { posted: false, reason: "eval", count: findings.length };
  }

  return await postFindings(findings);
}
```

The tool call stays in the trajectory, so the eval can still assert that the agent chose to post.

Source: /docs/guides/agent-to-agent.md

# Peer agents

A peer connection lets one agent ask an independent specialist for help. The
specialist keeps its own instructions, tools, and sessions. On Cursor hosting,
team-owned agents reach each other by deployment slug, and Agent SDK handles
routing and authentication for you.

## Delegate a question to a specialist

Ask the concierge about the weather, and it hands the question to the weather
agent and returns the answer.

```ts
// bot/mcp-connections/weather.ts
import { defineConnection } from "@grok/agent-sdk/connections";

export default defineConnection({
  agent: "weather-agent",
  description: "Delegate weather questions to the weather specialist.",
});
```

The filename, `weather.ts`, becomes the
[MCP server name](/docs/reference/connections.md#peer-mcp-connection), and `agent`
is the specialist's lowercase deployment slug. Give the concierge a one-way
routing rule, so the agents never pass a request back and forth:

```md
When a request needs current weather, ask the `weather` peer. Return its
answer.
```

Deploy both agents from pushed Git refs:

```bash
agent-sdk deploy --dir ./agents/weather-agent --slug weather-agent
agent-sdk deploy --dir ./agents/concierge --slug concierge
```

## Continue the specialist's session

The first `ask` returns `{ status, sessionId, reply }` as text. Pass that
`sessionId` on the next `ask` to continue the specialist's earlier work.

```ts
const first = await ctx.host.mcp.callTool("weather", "ask", {
  message: "What's the weather in Paris right now?",
});
const firstText = first.content.find((part) => part.type === "text");
if (firstText?.text === undefined) {
  throw new Error("weather ask returned no text payload");
}
const { sessionId } = JSON.parse(firstText.text) as { sessionId: string };

await ctx.host.mcp.callTool("weather", "ask", {
  message: "How does that compare with tomorrow?",
  sessionId,
});
```

If the specialist is still working, `ask` returns `status: "running"`, and
`check` waits for the answer.

```ts
await ctx.host.mcp.callTool("weather", "check", {
  sessionId,
  waitSeconds: 20,
});
```

## Call a peer tool directly

Use `call_tool` when you want to run a tool on a peer agent directly, without
starting a model turn on that agent. The peer needs at least one server tool,
and the call follows the
[direct-call rules](/docs/reference/tools.md#call-a-tool-without-a-model-turn).

```ts
const result = await ctx.host.mcp.callTool("weather", "call_tool", {
  toolName: "get_forecast",
  input: { city: "Paris" },
});
const part = result.content.find((item) => item.type === "text");
if (part?.text === undefined) {
  return { ok: false, forecast: null };
}
const payload = JSON.parse(part.text) as {
  isError?: boolean;
  result?: unknown;
};

return {
  ok: result.isError !== true && payload.isError !== true,
  forecast: payload.result ?? null,
};
```

## Try it locally

To try it locally, run both projects in one process:

```bash
agent-sdk dev ./agents
agent-sdk chat --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/concierge \
  --message "What's the weather in Paris right now?"
```

Locally, `agent` is the specialist's mount slug, usually its directory name.

## Peer or subagent?

Use a [subagent](/docs/reference/subagents.md) to split one agent's job into roles.
Use a peer when the specialist is a complete agent you also run on its own.

| | Subagent | Peer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context | Child role inside one agent | Independent agent and session |
| Tools and connections | Inherits the parent project | Owns its project surface |
| Reachability | Parent only | Local co-hosted agents, or declared deployments on the same team |

## Other hosts

To self-host, run the peers under one `agent-sdk` process, and if turns run on
remote workers, protect it with `--bearer-token` and set `--public-url` as
[Deployment](/docs/deployment.md) describes.

---

Source: /docs/guides/bitbucket.md

# Bitbucket agents

A Bitbucket agent wakes on pull request, comment, and push events from
Bitbucket Cloud or Data Center, then writes its results back to the
repository. Declare `onPullRequest`, `onPullRequestComment`, or `onPush`
on `bitbucketChannel()` for each event that should wake it.

## Connect a repository

Name the repository hook secret and list the repositories that may wake
the agent.

```ts
// bot/channels/bitbucket.ts
import { bitbucketChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/bitbucket";

export default bitbucketChannel({
  repos: ["acme/widgets"],
  webhookSecret: { secretName: "BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
});
```

Add a repository webhook for
`https://<your-host>/<slug>/v1/channels/bitbucket` with the same secret.
On Cursor hosting, a delivery with the wrong secret gets a `401` and
never reaches your agent. For Data Center, set the REST base and the API token:

```ts
export default bitbucketChannel({
  repos: ["PLATFORM/api"],
  webhookSecret: { secretName: "BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
  token: () => process.env.BITBUCKET_TOKEN ?? "",
  apiBaseUrl: "https://bitbucket.example.com/rest/api/1.0",
});
```

For Bitbucket Cloud, omit `apiBaseUrl`. To set the secrets on a deployment, see
[Add egress and secrets](/docs/deployment.md#add-egress-and-secrets).

For Bitbucket Cloud on Cursor hosting, you can skip the repository
webhook. Set `cursorAccount: { repos: ["acme/widgets"] }`, and events and
`ctx.bitbucket` calls go through your signed-in Cursor account.

## Review a pull request

When someone opens a pull request, or pushes new commits to a Data Center
pull request, the agent reads the diff and posts its review as a comment
on the pull request.

```ts
// bot/channels/bitbucket.ts
import {
  bitbucketChannel,
  defaultBitbucketAuth,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/bitbucket";
import { postPullRequestComment } from "../lib/bitbucket.js";

export default bitbucketChannel({
  repos: ["acme/widgets"],
  webhookSecret: { secretName: "BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
  onPullRequest: async (ctx, pullRequest) => {
    if (pullRequest.draft) {
      return null;
    }
    const hasNewCommits =
      pullRequest.action === "updated" &&
      pullRequest.previousHeadSha !== undefined &&
      pullRequest.previousHeadSha !== pullRequest.headSha;
    if (pullRequest.action !== "created" && !hasNewCommits) {
      return null;
    }

    const diff = await ctx.bitbucket.api.getPullRequestDiff(pullRequest.id);
    return {
      // `auth` starts a model turn running as the event sender.
      auth: defaultBitbucketAuth(ctx),
      message: `Review ${ctx.repository.fullName}#${pullRequest.id}.`,
      context: [`<bitbucket_diff>${diff}</bitbucket_diff>`],
    };
  },
  events: {
    async "message.completed"(event, channel, ctx) {
      if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
        return;
      }
      if (event.data.finishReason === "tool_call" || event.data.text === "") {
        return;
      }
      const pullRequestId = channel.state.pullRequestId;
      if (
        !channel.state.eventType?.startsWith("pullrequest:") ||
        pullRequestId === null
      ) {
        return;
      }
      await postPullRequestComment(channel.state, pullRequestId, event.data.text);
    },
  },
});
```

`postPullRequestComment` is a small helper you write in
`bot/lib/bitbucket.ts` that posts a comment through the Bitbucket API
with `BITBUCKET_TOKEN`. It uses the repository and pull request from the
session state, so the model never picks where the review goes.

Each hook returns `{ auth }`, `{ task }`, or `null`, as
[handler results](/docs/reference/channels.md#handler-results) describes.
All events on the same pull request go to the same session, so the agent
sees the whole conversation.

## Answer a pull-request comment

Skip the agent's own comments, and answer a comment that mentions the agent:

```ts
const AGENT_USERNAME = "cursor-reviewer";

onPullRequestComment: (ctx, comment) => {
  if (comment.author?.username === AGENT_USERNAME) {
    return null;
  }
  if (!comment.body.includes(`@${AGENT_USERNAME}`)) {
    return null;
  }
  return {
    auth: defaultBitbucketAuth(ctx),
    message: comment.body,
  };
},
```

Add this property to the same `bitbucketChannel()` as the review handler.

## Triage a push to `main`

Mark the new commit as in progress, then start the triage turn:

```ts
import {
  bitbucketChannelStateForEvent,
  defaultBitbucketAuth,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/bitbucket";
import { setPushTriageStatus } from "../lib/bitbucket.js";

onPush: (ctx, push) => {
  const change = push.changes.find(
    candidate =>
      candidate.name === "main" && candidate.after !== undefined
  );
  if (change?.after === undefined) {
    return null;
  }
  const sha = change.after;

  return {
    // `task` runs this host sequence after the webhook is acknowledged.
    task: async ({ send }) => {
      await ctx.bitbucket.setBuildStatus({
        sha,
        key: "cursor/push-triage",
        state: "INPROGRESS",
        name: "Cursor push triage",
        description: "Investigating push to main",
      });

      await send(`Triage push ${sha} on ${ctx.repository.fullName}.`, {
        auth: defaultBitbucketAuth(ctx),
        title: `Bitbucket push ${sha}`,
        state: {
          ...bitbucketChannelStateForEvent({
            repository: ctx.repository,
            headSha: sha,
            eventType: ctx.eventType,
          }),
        },
      });
    },
  };
},
```

When the turn ends, update that same status:

```ts
async "message.completed"(event, channel, ctx) {
  if (
    ctx.session.purpose !== "eval" &&
    channel.state.eventType === "repo:push" &&
    channel.state.headSha !== null &&
    event.data.finishReason !== "tool_call"
  ) {
    await setPushTriageStatus(
      channel.state,
      "SUCCESSFUL",
      "Push triage complete"
    );
    return;
  }

  // Continue with the pull-request reply branch from the first example.
},
async "turn.failed"(_event, channel, ctx) {
  if (
    ctx.session.purpose === "eval" ||
    channel.state.eventType !== "repo:push" ||
    channel.state.headSha === null
  ) {
    return;
  }
  await setPushTriageStatus(
    channel.state,
    "FAILED",
    "Push triage failed"
  );
},
```

This status reports the triage run, not the health of the pushed commit.

## Test with replay

Replay a pull request you can read against your local agent, or save the
payloads as fixtures. For Data Center, pass the full pull request URL.
[`bitbucket replay`](/docs/reference/cli.md#replay-other-webhooks) lists
every flag.

```text
agent-sdk dev
agent-sdk bitbucket replay acme/widgets#42 --events '*'
agent-sdk bitbucket replay acme/widgets#42 --events '*' --dry-run --fixtures-dir fixtures/bitbucket
```

---

Source: /docs/guides/cloud-agents.md

# Cloud agents

The `cursor-cloud-agents` extension lets an Agent SDK agent hand coding work to
Cursor cloud agents. A cloud agent works in a repository checkout and pushes
branches and pull requests while your agent keeps talking to the person.

## Mount it

```ts
// bot/extensions/cloud.ts
import cursorCloudAgents from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/cursor-cloud-agents";

export default cursorCloudAgents({
  cloud: {
    repos: [{ url: "https://github.com/acme/api", startingRef: "main" }],
    autoCreatePR: true,
  },
});
```

Launches run under the host's signed-in account (`agent-sdk login`,
`CURSOR_API_KEY`, or `CURSOR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY`) and spend its cloud-agent
budget.

## What the agent can do

With the extension mounted, the agent can launch a cloud agent on a repository
or pull request, check its status, read its conversation and edits, steer or
stop it, and list the agents it launched. A bundled skill teaches the model when
to delegate and how to write a brief a cloud agent can act on alone.

Each caller can only see and steer the cloud agents they launched. If every
caller uses the same bearer token, the extension treats them all as one person.
Use [authored auth](/docs/reference/channels.md#auth-policies) to keep callers
apart.

## Configure it

| Option | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `cloud` | Launch defaults for repositories, environment, and pull request behavior. |
| `cloud.repos` | The repositories the agent may hand work to, each with a default branch or pull request. Without it, launches run with no repository, so secrets in `cloud.envVars` never reach a repository you didn't list. |
| `cloud.teamMcpServers` | Up to 50 team MCP server names that launched agents may use, matched case-insensitively. Omit it to allow every team server the account can use. Personal servers and `cloud.mcpServers` aren't filtered. |
| `model` | The model launched agents run. Omit it to use the account default. |
| `apiKey` | A Cursor API key to launch with instead of the host's own. |

## Adjust it

To remove a capability such as sending follow-ups, mount the extension as a
directory and disable that tool. See
[Adjust a mounted extension](/docs/reference/extensions.md#adjust-a-mounted-extension).

---

Source: /docs/guides/convert-automation.md

# Convert a Cursor Automation

Convert a dashboard Automation when you want to edit its behavior as code, test
it locally, or deploy it as an Agent SDK project. To change only the prompt or
the trigger, stay in the dashboard.

## Convert and run locally

`init --from automation:<url>` creates a project with the Automation's prompt,
model, and any schedules, channels, and account connections it can represent.
It prints warnings and setup steps for the rest.

```text
agent-sdk login
agent-sdk init --from \
  automation:https://cursor.com/automations/0a1b2c3d-0000-1111-2222-333344445555

cd nightly-triage
agent-sdk dev
```

Try the agent in the playground before you reconnect a live trigger. The
[CLI reference](/docs/reference/cli.md#convert-automation) covers the other
options.

## Reconnect account-backed actions

For an HTTP or SSE MCP server, the converter writes a connection by name,
without its URL or credentials. Connect the same server under MCP in Cursor,
sign in on the local host, and the agent uses its tools through your account.

```ts
// bot/mcp-connections/linear.ts
import { defineConnection } from "@grok/agent-sdk/connections";

export default defineConnection({
  cursorAccount: true,
  servers: ["Linear"],
});
```

## Bring a Slack trigger online

Once you create the [Slack app](/docs/guides/slack.md), the agent answers mentions in the
same thread. For a channel watch, also subscribe the app to channel posts:

```text
agent-sdk slack create --dir . --channel-posts
```

The converter keeps the watch allowlist. If a warning says the Automation also
filtered messages by text, add that check to the channel's `onChannelPost` hook.

## Bring a GitHub trigger online

The generated GitHub channel keeps simple filters such as PR actions, branches, and repositories, and a hook whose condition depended on dashboard-only context returns `null` until you replace it. This converted CI trigger wakes only when the suite fails:

```ts
import {
  defaultGitHubAuth,
  githubChannel,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";

export default githubChannel({
  cursorAccount: { repos: ["acme/api"] },
  webhookEvents: ["check_suite"],
  onCheckSuite: (ctx, suite) => {
    if (suite.conclusion !== "failure") {
      return null;
    }
    return { auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) };
  },
});
```

Replay a failing PR before you connect live delivery:

```text
agent-sdk github replay acme/api#42 --dir . --events '*' --conclusion failure
```

Cursor-account delivery carries PR and comment events. Push, issue, and CI
triggers need webhook delivery through a GitHub App or `github forward`, as the
[GitHub guide](/docs/guides/github.md) explains.

## Work through the checklist

The converter doesn't carry every behavior over. Before you turn on a live
trigger, go through the warnings and setup steps it prints:

- A setup step names something you have to connect or configure.
- A `Verify:` step names a dashboard action with no matching tool. Run the agent
  and confirm the same external write happens.
- A `.todo.md` file marks a connection you have to replace.
- Credentials, webhook registration, and Automation memory never carry over.

Keep the source Automation enabled while you work, and when you [deploy](/docs/deployment.md), disable it before you turn on the same live triggers. The converter doesn't support Cursor-managed Automations.

---

Source: /docs/guides/github.md

# GitHub agents

A GitHub agent wakes from repo events, reads the latest PR and CI state,
then writes back reviews, comments, checks, or pushes. Every wake for the
same pull request resumes one session, so the open, later comments, and
CI results share one conversation.

Connect GitHub in Cursor for the repos you care about (Settings or
[cursor.com/dashboard](https://cursor.com/dashboard)), then sign the host
in with `agent-sdk login`. `cursorAccount` reuses that connection for
events and API calls, so you don't need a public webhook URL, a GitHub
App, or a personal access token.

For a complete reviewer or issue triager, start from the
[review and triage templates](/docs/templates/reviews.md).

## Review a pull request

When someone opens a pull request or marks it ready for review, the agent
starts a turn, reads the change, and posts its verdict as a review.

```ts
// bot/channels/github.ts
import { defaultGitHubAuth, githubChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";

export default githubChannel({
  // Skip the agent's own comments so replies don't re-trigger it.
  botName: "my-agent",
  cursorAccount: { repos: ["acme/checkout"] },
  onPullRequest: (ctx, pr) => {
    if (pr.draft) {
      return null;
    }
    if (pr.action !== "opened" && pr.action !== "ready_for_review") {
      return null;
    }
    // `auth` starts a model turn running as the sender.
    return { auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) };
  },
});
```

```ts
// bot/tools/submit_review.ts
import { parseGitHubPrContinuationKey } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineTool({
  description:
    "Post the review decision on this session's pull request. Call once.",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    verdict: z.enum(["approve", "request_changes"]),
    summary: z
      .string()
      .describe("One or two sentences explaining the verdict."),
  }),
  async execute({ verdict, summary }, ctx) {
    if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
      return { posted: false, reason: "eval" };
    }
    const ref = parseGitHubPrContinuationKey(ctx.session.continuationKey ?? "");
    if (ref === undefined) {
      throw new Error("submit_review requires a GitHub pull request session");
    }

    let event: "APPROVE" | "REQUEST_CHANGES" = "REQUEST_CHANGES";
    if (verdict === "approve") {
      event = "APPROVE";
    }
    const octokit = await ctx.host.github.getOctokit();
    await octokit.rest.pulls.createReview({
      owner: ref.owner,
      repo: ref.repo,
      pull_number: ref.number,
      event,
      body: summary,
    });
    return { posted: true, pr: `${ref.owner}/${ref.repo}#${ref.number}` };
  },
});
```

The event only tells you that the pull request changed. Read the title,
files, and checks during the turn.

## Answer a mention

`onComment` replaces the default `@botName` gate. Return a turn when the
comment is for this agent, then post the reply from a tool.

```ts
onComment: (ctx, comment) => {
  if (!comment.body.includes("@my-agent")) {
    return null;
  }
  return { auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) };
},
```

```ts
// bot/tools/reply.ts
import { parseGitHubPrContinuationKey } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineTool({
  description: "Post a comment on this session's pull request.",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    body: z.string().describe("Markdown to post on the PR timeline."),
  }),
  async execute({ body }, ctx) {
    if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
      return { posted: false, reason: "eval" };
    }
    const ref = parseGitHubPrContinuationKey(ctx.session.continuationKey ?? "");
    if (ref === undefined) {
      throw new Error("reply requires a GitHub pull request session");
    }

    const octokit = await ctx.host.github.getOctokit();
    await octokit.rest.issues.createComment({
      owner: ref.owner,
      repo: ref.repo,
      issue_number: ref.number,
      body,
    });
    return { posted: true };
  },
});
```

The tool reads the pull request from the session, so the model never
picks where the comment goes.

## Triage a failing check

When CI fails, this hook labels the pull request with host code and no
model turn. Return `{ auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) }` instead when the
agent should read the logs and decide what to do.

```ts
onCheckSuite: (ctx, suite) => {
  if (suite.conclusion !== "failure") {
    return null;
  }
  // `task` runs host code instead of a model turn.
  return { task: () => labelFailure(ctx, suite) };
},
```

```ts
async function labelFailure(ctx, suite) {
  const pr = suite.pullRequests[0];
  if (pr === undefined) {
    return;
  }
  const octokit = await ctx.github.getOctokit();
  await octokit.rest.issues.addLabels({
    owner: ctx.repository.owner,
    repo: ctx.repository.name,
    issue_number: pr.number,
    labels: ["ci-failed"],
  });
}
```

## Events

Declare a hook for each event that should wake the agent:
`onPullRequest`, `onComment`, `onIssue`, `onCheckSuite`, `onCheckRun`,
`onWorkflowRun`, `onStatus`, and the catch-all `onEvent`. Each hook
returns `{ auth }`, `{ task }`, or `null`, as
[handler results](/docs/reference/channels.md#handler-results) describes.

## Choose watched repositories

The examples above list their repositories with
`cursorAccount: { repos: [...] }`, and every repository in one channel
must share one GitHub owner. To keep the list out of source, set
`cursorAccount: true` and pass `--repo` to `agent-sdk serve`. A hosted
deployment watches the repositories you pass to `agent-sdk deploy` in
both cases.

```text
agent-sdk serve --dir . --cursor-events \
  --repo acme/checkout --repo acme/payments
agent-sdk deploy --dir . \
  --cursor-events-repo acme/checkout \
  --cursor-events-repo acme/payments
```

Each deploy replaces the previous list, so pass every repository each
time. Use [`agent-sdk deployment update`](/docs/reference/cli.md#deployment-update)
to change the list without redeploying.

## Call GitHub from deterministic code via `ctx`

With `cursorAccount`, hooks (`ctx.github.getOctokit()`) and tools (`ctx.host.github.getOctokit()`) share one credential. Hooks can also use `ctx.thread.post()`, `ctx.repository`, and `ctx.conversation`.

This hook reads the pull request, skips a draft, and posts before the model turn:

```ts
onPullRequest: async (ctx, pr) => {
  if (pr.action !== "opened") {
    return null;
  }
  const octokit = await ctx.github.getOctokit();
  const { data } = await octokit.rest.pulls.get({
    owner: ctx.repository.owner,
    repo: ctx.repository.name,
    pull_number: pr.number,
  });
  if (data.draft) {
    return null;
  }
  await ctx.thread.post(`Reviewing ${pr.url}`);
  return { auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) };
},
```

## Batch events

GitHub can send many events for one pull request within a few seconds. Coalesce them per pull request:

```ts
const pending = new Map();

function enqueue(pr, flush) {
  const key = `${pr.owner}/${pr.repo}#${pr.number}`;
  const existing = pending.get(key);
  if (existing !== undefined) {
    clearTimeout(existing);
  }
  pending.set(
    key,
    setTimeout(() => {
      pending.delete(key);
      flush();
    }, 3_000)
  );
}
```

Persist that buffer across restarts, and drop it when the pull request closes.

## Test with replay

`agent-sdk github replay` reads a pull request you can access and posts
GitHub-shaped events to your channel.

```text
agent-sdk github replay https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42 --dir . --action opened

# Replay everything the channel listens for, with CI failing
agent-sdk github replay acme/checkout#42 --dir . --events '*' --conclusion failure

# Save the payloads as fixtures instead of posting them
agent-sdk github replay acme/checkout#42 --dir . --events '*' --dry-run --fixtures-dir fixtures/github
```

## Other hosts

The same hooks work on GitHub Enterprise Server, and on github.com when
you already receive GitHub webhooks yourself. Point the channel at your
server:

```ts
export default githubChannel({
  api: {
    apiBaseUrl: "https://github.example.com/api/v3",
  },
  credentials: {
    token: { secretName: "GITHUB_TOKEN" },
    webhookSecret: { secretName: "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
  },
});
```

Add a repository webhook for
`https://<your-host>/<slug>/v1/channels/github` with the same secret.
On Cursor hosting, a delivery with a missing or wrong signature gets a
`401` and never reaches your agent. Event pull and `github replay` only
reach github.com, so test Enterprise Server with saved fixtures.

Pass each credential as `{ secretName: "NAME" }`. When you run locally, the channel reads the environment variable with that name, and on Cursor hosting it reads the deployment secret with that name. To set those secrets on a deployment, see [Add egress and secrets](/docs/deployment.md#add-egress-and-secrets).

## Related

- [Build a PR reviewer](/docs/quickstart.md) covers the full loop.
- Ask a coding agent to follow the `bdk-github` skill for the GitHub setup steps.

---

Source: /docs/guides/gitlab.md

# GitLab agents

A GitLab agent wakes on merge request, note, and pipeline events from
GitLab.com or a self-managed server, then writes its results back to the
project. Declare `onMergeRequest`, `onNote`, or `onPipeline` on
`gitlabChannel()` for each event that should wake it.

## Connect a project

Name the project hook secret and list the projects that may wake the
agent. Set `apiBaseUrl` for a self-managed server, and leave it out for
GitLab.com.

```ts
// bot/channels/gitlab.ts
import { gitlabChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/gitlab";

export default gitlabChannel({
  projects: ["acme/platform"],
  webhookSecret: { secretName: "GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
  apiBaseUrl: "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4",
});
```

Add a project webhook for
`https://<your-host>/<slug>/v1/channels/gitlab` with the same secret. On
Cursor hosting, a delivery with the wrong secret gets a `401` and never
reaches your agent. `ctx.gitlab` calls the API with the token in
`GITLAB_TOKEN`. To set both secrets on a deployment, see
[Add egress and secrets](/docs/deployment.md#add-egress-and-secrets).

For GitLab.com on Cursor hosting, you can skip the project webhook. Set
`cursorAccount: { projects: ["acme/platform"] }`, and events and
`ctx.gitlab` calls go through your signed-in Cursor account.

## Review a merge request

Read the latest diff, then post the finished review as a note:

```ts
// bot/channels/gitlab.ts
import {
  createGitLabApi,
  defaultGitLabAuth,
  gitlabChannel,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/gitlab";
import { postMergeRequestNote } from "../lib/gitlab.js";

export default gitlabChannel({
  projects: ["acme/platform"],
  onMergeRequest: async (ctx, mergeRequest) => {
    if (mergeRequest.draft) {
      return null;
    }
    const hasNewCommits =
      mergeRequest.action === "update" && mergeRequest.oldrev !== undefined;
    if (
      mergeRequest.action !== "open" &&
      mergeRequest.action !== "reopen" &&
      !hasNewCommits
    ) {
      return null;
    }

    const api = createGitLabApi(
      ctx.gitlab,
      ctx.project.pathWithNamespace
    );
    const diffs = await api.listMergeRequestDiffs(mergeRequest.iid);
    return {
      // `auth` starts a model turn running as the event sender.
      auth: defaultGitLabAuth(ctx),
      message: `Review ${ctx.project.pathWithNamespace}!${mergeRequest.iid}.`,
      context: [`<gitlab_diffs>${JSON.stringify(diffs)}</gitlab_diffs>`],
    };
  },
  events: {
    async "message.completed"(event, channel, ctx) {
      if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
        return;
      }
      if (event.data.finishReason === "tool_call" || event.data.text === "") {
        return;
      }
      const mergeRequestIid = channel.state.mergeRequestIid;
      if (
        (channel.state.eventType !== "merge_request" &&
          channel.state.eventType !== "note") ||
        mergeRequestIid === null
      ) {
        return;
      }
      await postMergeRequestNote(
        channel.state.projectPath,
        mergeRequestIid,
        event.data.text
      );
    },
  },
});
```

`postMergeRequestNote` is a helper you write that posts through the GitLab API with `GITLAB_TOKEN`. It uses the project and merge request stored from the event.

## Answer a note

Skip the agent's own notes, and answer a note that mentions the agent:

```ts
const AGENT_USERNAME = "cursor-reviewer";

onNote: (ctx, note) => {
  if (note.author?.username === AGENT_USERNAME) {
    return null;
  }
  if (!note.body.includes(`@${AGENT_USERNAME}`)) {
    return null;
  }
  return {
    auth: defaultGitLabAuth(ctx),
    message: note.body,
  };
},
```

Add this property to the same `gitlabChannel()` as the review handler.

## Triage a failed pipeline

When a pipeline fails, the example marks the commit status as `running`
and starts a triage turn. When the turn finishes, it sets the status to
success or failure.

```ts
// bot/channels/gitlab.ts
import {
  defaultGitLabAuth,
  gitlabChannel,
  gitlabChannelStateForEvent,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/gitlab";
import { setPipelineTriageStatus } from "../lib/gitlab.js";

export default gitlabChannel({
  projects: ["acme/platform"],
  webhookSecret: { secretName: "GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET" },
  onPipeline: (ctx, pipeline) => {
    if (pipeline.status !== "failed" || pipeline.sha === undefined) {
      return null;
    }
    const sha = pipeline.sha;
    return {
      // `task` runs host code, and `send` starts the model turn.
      task: async ({ send }) => {
        await ctx.gitlab.setCommitStatus({
          sha,
          state: "running",
          name: "cursor/pipeline-triage",
          description: "Investigating failed pipeline",
        });
        await send(`Triage failed GitLab pipeline ${pipeline.id}.`, {
          auth: defaultGitLabAuth(ctx),
          state: {
            ...gitlabChannelStateForEvent({
              project: ctx.project,
              headSha: sha,
              eventType: ctx.eventType,
            }),
          },
        });
      },
    };
  },
  events: {
    async "message.completed"(event, channel, ctx) {
      if (
        ctx.session.purpose === "eval" ||
        channel.state.eventType !== "pipeline" ||
        channel.state.headSha === null ||
        event.data.finishReason === "tool_call"
      ) {
        return;
      }
      await setPipelineTriageStatus(channel.state.projectPath, channel.state.headSha, "success");
    },
    async "turn.failed"(_event, channel, ctx) {
      if (
        ctx.session.purpose === "eval" ||
        channel.state.eventType !== "pipeline" ||
        channel.state.headSha === null
      ) {
        return;
      }
      await setPipelineTriageStatus(channel.state.projectPath, channel.state.headSha, "failed");
    },
  },
});
```

`setPipelineTriageStatus` is a small helper you write in
`bot/lib/gitlab.ts`. It updates the same `cursor/pipeline-triage` status
through the GitLab API with `GITLAB_TOKEN`, using the project and commit
from the session state, so the model never picks where it writes.

Each hook returns `{ auth }`, `{ task }`, or `null`, as
[handler results](/docs/reference/channels.md#handler-results) describes.
Every event and note on one merge request resumes the same session.

## Test with replay

Replay a merge request you can read against your local agent, or save the
payloads as fixtures.
[`gitlab replay`](/docs/reference/cli.md#replay-other-webhooks) lists every
flag.

```text
agent-sdk dev
agent-sdk gitlab replay acme/platform!42 --events pipeline --conclusion failed
agent-sdk gitlab replay acme/platform!42 --events '*' --dry-run --fixtures-dir fixtures/gitlab
```

---

Source: /docs/guides/improve.md

# Self-improvement

The `improve` extension lets an agent turn "change how you work" into a change
to its own source. The agent writes a brief, a Cursor cloud agent edits a
checkout and opens a pull request, and the agent reports the pull request.

## Mount it

Mount [Cloud agents](/docs/guides/cloud-agents.md) with the agent's own repository in
`cloud.repos`, then mount `improve` with its source directory.

```ts
// bot/extensions/cloud.ts
import cursorCloudAgents from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/cursor-cloud-agents";

export default cursorCloudAgents({
  cloud: {
    repos: [{ url: "https://github.com/acme/agents", startingRef: "main" }],
    autoCreatePR: true,
  },
});
```

```ts
// bot/extensions/improve.ts
import improve from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/improve";

export default improve({
  repo: "https://github.com/acme/agents",
  path: "agents/concierge",
  ref: "main",
});
```

`improve` adds the `improve__yourself` skill and no tools.

## Ask for one change

Say what to change, how to tell it worked, and what must not change.

> Improve yourself. Stop opening incident replies with a summary. Start with
> the decision, keep the existing evidence bullets, and preserve every current
> eval.

The agent launches one cloud agent and reports its URL. When the pull request
opens, the agent tells you what changed and which checks passed.

## Review, merge, then deploy

The agent can open a pull request, but it can't merge or deploy. Someone on your
team reviews and merges it, and the change goes live on your next deploy.
Afterward, repeat the original request to confirm the change.

## Configure it

- `repo` is the source repository URL.
- `path` is the agent's directory in that repository.
- `ref` is the branch new pull requests target, `main` by default.
- `notes` adds guidance to every brief, such as a required test command.
- `deploy` tells the skill who deploys a merged change and when.

Validation checks only the shape of `repo` and `path`, so make sure they match
the deployed agent and `cloud.repos`.

---

Source: /docs/guides/jev.md

# Use Jev in review tools

> [!WARNING]
> Experimental. `@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/jev` is experimental. Its
> exports and behavior can change in any release, without a deprecation
> period.

Use Jev when a review workflow needs a typed decision instead of prose. Jev
returns a choice, a score, or a probability, and your TypeScript decides what
happens next.

Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, then mount the extension. The default model is
`jev-latest`.

```ts
// bot/extensions/jev.ts
import jev from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/jev";

export default jev();
```

On Cursor hosting, the mount adds `api.typesafe.ai` to egress and
`TYPESAFE_API_KEY` to the expected secrets. Without the mount,
[add `api.typesafe.ai`](/docs/deployment.md#add-egress-and-secrets) to
`hosting.egressDomains` yourself.

## Start only the review turns you need

Call Jev from a channel hook before a model turn starts. This hook asks Jev
whether a new pull request needs security review, based on its title, body, and
file names. Below the threshold, the hook returns `null`, so the agent doesn't
run or post anything.

```ts
// bot/channels/github.ts
import {
  defaultGitHubAuth,
  githubChannel,
} from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";
import { above, decide } from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/jev";

export default githubChannel({
  cursorAccount: { repos: ["acme/checkout"] },
  onPullRequest: async (ctx, pr) => {
    if (pr.action !== "opened" && pr.action !== "ready_for_review") {
      return null;
    }

    const octokit = await ctx.github.getOctokit();
    const files = await octokit.paginate(octokit.rest.pulls.listFiles, {
      owner: ctx.repository.owner,
      repo: ctx.repository.name,
      pull_number: pr.number,
    });
    const answers = await decide({
      state: {
        title: pr.title,
        body: pr.body,
        files: files.map(file => file.filename),
      },
      questions: {
        review: {
          type: "boolean",
          instructions: "Does this change touch auth, permissions, secrets, or external input?",
        },
      },
    });

    if (!above(answers.review, 0.8)) {
      return null;
    }
    return { auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx) };
  },
});
```

## Filter findings before you post them

Let the model draft a finding, then ask Jev whether it's a real bug in the new
code. The tool posts only the drafts that clear your threshold.

```ts
// bot/tools/post_finding.ts
import { parseGitHubPrContinuationKey } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";
import { above, decide } from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/jev";
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineTool({
  description: "Post one security finding on this session's pull request.",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    summary: z.string(),
    draft: z.string().describe("The finding, in one or two sentences."),
  }),
  async execute({ summary, draft }, ctx) {
    if (ctx.session.purpose === "eval") {
      return { posted: false, reason: "eval" };
    }

    const ref = parseGitHubPrContinuationKey(ctx.session.continuationKey ?? "");
    if (ref === undefined) {
      throw new Error("post_finding requires a GitHub pull request session");
    }

    const answers = await decide({
      state: { summary, draft },
      questions: {
        real: {
          type: "boolean",
          instructions: "Is the draft an exploitable bug in the new code?",
        },
      },
    });

    if (!above(answers.real, 0.85)) {
      return { posted: false, reason: "clean" };
    }

    const octokit = await ctx.host.github.getOctokit();
    await octokit.rest.pulls.createReview({
      owner: ref.owner,
      repo: ref.repo,
      pull_number: ref.number,
      event: "COMMENT",
      body: draft,
    });
    return { posted: true };
  },
});
```

## Approve changes by risk tier

Ask Jev for one risk tier. Approve only a confident `very-low` or `low`.

```ts
import { decide, needsHuman } from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/jev";

const answers = await decide({
  state: { title, summary },
  questions: {
    risk: {
      type: "choice",
      instructions: "What risk tier is this pull request?",
      criteria: {
        "very-low": "docs, formatting, or a mechanical rename",
        low: "a local change with tests and no new trust boundary",
        medium: "auth, billing, or a behavior change callers depend on",
        high: "a likely exploit, data loss, or a broken public contract",
      },
    },
  },
});

const tier = answers.risk.choice;
if (needsHuman(answers.risk) || tier === "medium" || tier === "high") {
  return { verdict: "hold", tier };
}
return { verdict: "approve", tier };
```

Your tool resolves the pull request from the session and posts that verdict, as the [Agentic Owners template](/docs/templates/agentic-owners.md) does.

## Write tools with Jev

Call `decide` to get the answer map, or `evaluate` to get `{ answers }`. Use a
boolean for a yes-or-no gate, a choice for a closed set such as risk tiers, and
a score for an ordered rubric. `above` returns `true` when a probability or
score meets your threshold. `needsHuman` returns `true` when the answer's
confidence falls below `0.7` by default. Calibrate both on pull requests you've
already labeled.

Ask Jev one question per call, and write the rule that combines the answers in
your own code.

## Let the agent ask Jev

The mount also gives the model a read-only tool named `<namespace>__evaluate`,
which is `jev__evaluate` with the mount shown earlier. The model can call it
during a turn, and it never posts or approves anything. When the answer and the
write belong together, call `decide` inside a project tool instead.

## Choose what to mount

Mounting Jev also adds two skills. `jev__questions` teaches the model to write
atomic questions and read the answers, and `jev__gated-write` teaches it to put
`decide` and the write in one server tool. Set `harnessTools: false` to keep Jev
inside your own tools, or `skills: false` if your agent has its own Jev
instructions.

```ts
export default jev({ harnessTools: false, skills: true });
```

Neither switch removes the exported helpers, so project tools can still import
`decide`, `above`, and `needsHuman`.

---

Source: /docs/guides/mcp-oauth.md

# Connect a private MCP server with OAuth

Host MCP OAuth lets the machine running your agent authorize a remote
MCP server without putting tokens in your source or workspace.

## Use a private MCP tool locally

Declare the server and authorize it once in the browser.

```ts
// bot/mcp-connections/inventory.ts
import { defineConnection } from "@grok/agent-sdk/connections";

export default defineConnection({
  url: "https://mcp.example.com/inventory",
  oauth: true,
  advertiseTools: true,
});
```

```bash
agent-sdk mcp oauth inventory
```

The filename is the connection name. If you change the server URL, run
`mcp oauth` again.

## Connect on first use

Without a prior `mcp oauth`, the first call to the server pauses the
turn, and the playground shows **Connect**. Finish the browser flow,
and the call retries in the running process.

A turn waits for Connect only when a person can click it:

- A playground or HTTP chat turn.
- A Slack message, when the channel shows Connect through
  `slackChannel({ toolApprovals: true })` or `buildToolApprovalEvents`
  in `events`.

The wait stops after 10 minutes or when the turn is interrupted.
Schedules, reminders, webhooks, evals, and Slack channels without
Connect don't wait. A required connection fails the call with
`Reconnect <connection>`, and an `optional` one is skipped, even in the
playground. Authorize those ahead of time with `mcp oauth`.

## Keep privileged tools behind a wrapper

The model never sees a connection under `bot/host-connections/`. A
server tool reaches it through `ctx.host.mcp` and exposes one narrow
operation.

```ts
// bot/host-connections/inventory.ts
import { defineConnection } from "@grok/agent-sdk/connections";

export default defineConnection({
  url: "https://mcp.example.com/inventory",
  oauth: true,
  tools: ["lookup_stock"],
});
```

```ts
// bot/tools/get_stock.ts
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineTool({
  description: "Read stock for one approved region.",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    sku: z.string(),
    region: z.enum(["us-east", "us-west"]),
  }),
  async execute(input, ctx) {
    const result = await ctx.host.mcp.callTool(
      "inventory",
      "lookup_stock",
      input
    );
    return {
      ok: result.isError !== true,
      stock: result.structuredContent ?? null,
    };
  },
});
```

## Use an OAuth server from a hosted agent

Tokens from `mcp oauth` stay on the machine that authorized them. For a
Cursor-hosted agent, add the server under MCP in the Cursor dashboard,
reach it through a
[`cursorAccount: true` connection](/docs/reference/connections.md#cursor-account-mcp-connection),
and connect it from [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents).
Anyone who can use the agent can use that connection, so narrow its
`servers` list.

## Choose where credentials live

| Connection | Credentials live in | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cursorAccount: true` | Cursor's backend | You connected the server in the Cursor dashboard |
| `url` with `oauth: true` | The serve host | The serve host should own access |
| `url` with `headers` | Your secrets | The server takes an API key or bearer token |

Host OAuth can't share a connection with per-session `auth`, which
gives each caller its own downstream identity.

## Related

- Follow the `bdk-mcp-auth` skill, then run `agent-sdk mcp oauth <connection>`.
- [MCP connections](/docs/reference/connections.md)

---

Source: /docs/guides/migrate.md

# Migrate an early-alpha project to architecture v2

Use this guide only for an Agent SDK project deployed on architecture v1 during
the early alpha. Every other project already runs on v2.

## Check whether your project needs migration

Your project needs migration if any of these is true:

- `package.json` depends on `@cursor/july`.
- A script or CI job runs the early-alpha CLI.
- The agent sets `architecture: "v1"` or `runtime: "grokbot"`.
- The project has `bot/storage.ts` or `agent/storage.ts`.
- An SCM channel credential is a literal value.
- Code uses a `/v1` continuation selector.
- A reminder uses an anonymous `run` or `until` function.
- A peer connection reads its URL from a `*_MCP_URL` secret.
- `agent-sdk deployment get <slug>` doesn't print `architecture: v2`.

`agent-sdk migrate` checks the source for these signals and prints
`Nothing to migrate.` when it finds none. It doesn't check scripts, CI jobs, or
the hosted deployment.

To swap the early-alpha package, run:

```bash
npm uninstall @cursor/july
npm install @grok/agent-sdk@latest
```

An existing `agent/` folder still works.

## Start the migration

Commit and push the source first. `agent-sdk migrate` starts a Cursor cloud
agent on that pushed ref, and the agent opens a pull request without deploying.

```bash
agent-sdk login
agent-sdk migrate --dir .
```

To migrate a pushed source outside your checkout, pass `--repo`, `--ref`, and
`--path`. The [CLI reference](/docs/reference/cli.md#migrate) lists every flag.

You can also ask a coding agent in your checkout to follow the bundled `bdk-migrate-v2` skill. If the project
relies on a v1 capability that has no v2 path, the agent stops and names the
blocker.

## Review the pull request

Before you merge, check that the pull request:

- Uses `@grok/agent-sdk` and `agent-sdk`, and removes `architecture: "v1"`.
- Moves durable state to `ctx.host.kv` or `ctx.host.files`, reads secrets inside
  the handler that needs them, and expects hosted routes to return `202`.
- Passes every SCM credential as `{ secretName: "NAME" }`. `agent-sdk validate`
  warns about a literal or `process.env` getter while `architecture: "v1"` is
  set, and fails once you remove it.
- Replaces each peer URL secret, such as `BUILDER_MCP_URL`, with
  `defineConnection({ agent: "<slug>" })`. Check each slug and any TODO the
  agent left.
- Lists unsupported behavior, follow-ups, and the checks it ran or handed off.

## Choose a cutover

| Cutover | What happens | Choose it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same slug | v2 copies the v1 secrets and replaces v1 once it starts. You can't undo it, and it deletes v1's hosted sessions, KV, files, and eval runs. | A short outage and an empty v2 state are fine. |
| New slug | v1 keeps serving while you test v2. Move senders to the new URL, then delete v1. | You use Slack, webhooks, or hosted state. |

With a new slug, point the trial at a test repository so the two deployments
don't both act on the same events.

## Deploy after merge

Deploy from the merged, pushed ref. Reuse every `--cursor-events-repo` value
from v1, and move every `--allow-domain` value into `hosting.egressDomains`.

```bash
agent-sdk deploy --dir . --slug <existing-or-new-slug>
```

Then follow the checklist that `agent-sdk migrate` printed:

1. Deploy each agent folder separately by running
   `agent-sdk deploy --dir <agent-folder>` once for each one.
2. For each Slack agent, run
   `agent-sdk slack create --env prod --dir <agent-folder>`. Then uninstall the
   old app and invite the new bot to its channels.
3. For a [peer connection](/docs/guides/agent-to-agent.md), deploy both agents to the same
   team. Then delete each peer URL secret the pull request lists with
   `agent-sdk secret delete <slug> NAME`.
4. For a new slug, add each secret with `agent-sdk secret set <slug> NAME`. It
   applies without a redeploy.

Finally, [verify a hosted turn](/docs/deployment.md).

---

Source: /docs/guides/opentelemetry.md

# OpenTelemetry

Agent SDK sends traces, metrics, and logs to an OTLP collector when you
set the `OTEL_*` variables. Record your own with `@opentelemetry/api`.

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel.example.com
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer%20$OTEL_TOKEN"
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=incident-agent
agent-sdk serve --dir . --dev
```

- The default protocol is `http/protobuf`. `http/json` also works, and
  `grpc` logs a warning and falls back to `http/protobuf`.
- Metrics use delta temporality. Grafana Cloud and Prometheus reject
  delta, so set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE=cumulative`
  when you export to either one.
- If you don't set an endpoint, Agent SDK doesn't export anything.
- You can create a meter, tracer, or logger at the top of
  `bot/agent.ts`, and it will use Agent SDK's providers.

## Variables

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | Base URL. Appends `/v1/traces`, `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/logs`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` | Traces URL, used as written. Overrides the base URL. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | Metrics URL, used as written. Overrides the base URL. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT` | Logs URL, used as written. Overrides the base URL. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | Sent on every export. URL-encode values. Reread on each export. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `http/protobuf` (default) or `http/json`. |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `service.name`. Defaults to the agent name, then `unknown_service:node`. |
| `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` | `service.namespace`, `service.version`, `deployment.environment.name`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE` | `delta` (default), `cumulative`, or `lowmemory`. |
| `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` | `otlp` exports logs. Unset, `none`, and `console` do not. |
| `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` | `true` turns export off. |
| `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER` | `none` turns traces off. |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` | `none` turns metrics off. |
| `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS` | `1` adds prompt text to log records. |
| `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT` | `1` adds tool payloads to log records. |

## Hosted agents

```ts
export default defineAgent({
  hosting: {
    egressDomains: ["otlp-gateway-prod-us-east-0.grafana.net"],
    secretNames: [
      "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT",
      "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS",
      "OTEL_SERVICE_NAME",
    ],
  },
});
```

`service.name` is fixed by the first export, so redeploy to change it.

## Record and tag

```ts
import { metrics, trace } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import { logs } from "@opentelemetry/api-logs";
import { currentConversationId } from "@grok/agent-sdk/otel";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("incident-agent");
const lookups = metrics.getMeter("incident-agent").createCounter("incident.lookups");
const logger = logs.getLogger("incident-agent");

lookups.add(1, { "cursor.conversation.id": currentConversationId() });
```

Spans started during a turn get `cursor.conversation.id`, and a metric
gets it only when you set it.

To tag a whole turn, call `ctx.telemetry` from a tool. Spans in the
turn get the trace keys, Agent SDK's log records get the log keys, and
`cursor.token.usage` gets the metric keys. Outside a tool, use
`telemetry` from `@grok/agent-sdk/telemetry`.

```ts
async execute({ key }, ctx) {
  ctx.telemetry.setTraceAttributes({ "work.item": key });
  ctx.telemetry.setMetricAttributes({ "work.item": key });
  ctx.telemetry.setLogAttributes({ "work.item": key });
  return await jira.getIssue(key);
}
```

Grafana renames a `.` in a metric key to `_`.

```promql
sum by (work_item) (cursor_token_usage_total)
```

- Each distinct metric value is a new series, so never use a per-turn
  ID, a secret, an email, or a raw user ID.
- A session holds up to 32 keys of each kind, with keys up to 128
  characters and values up to 256.

## Limits

- Agent SDK doesn't support custom span processors, samplers, views,
  your own OpenTelemetry SDK, or library auto-instrumentation. It reads
  `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` and `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` once at
  startup, so restart the process after you change either one.
- Import Agent SDK before any other OpenTelemetry setup. Otherwise the
  turn's tags may not reach your spans.

## Migrating from serve({ otel })

Delete `serve({ otel })`, `bot/otel.ts`, `bot/instrumentation.ts`, and
any `defineOtel` call. Set these variables instead.

| Old option | Set this instead |
| --- | --- |
| `serviceName` | `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` |
| `serviceVersion` | `service.version` in `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` |
| `resourceAttributes` | `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`, comma-separated, URL-encoded values |
| `exporters[].url` | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (appends `/v1/traces`, `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/logs`) |
| `exporters[].url` with `signals` | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT`, or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT`, used as written |
| `exporters[].headers` | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, comma-separated, URL-encoded values |
| `exporters[].protocol` | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL`, or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_PROTOCOL`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_PROTOCOL`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_PROTOCOL` |
| `exporters[].signals` | The per-signal URL. `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=none`, `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none`, or `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none` stops that signal. |
| `traces: false` | `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=none` |
| `traces: true` | Leave `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER` unset. Traces start when an endpoint is set. |
| `traces.sampleRatio` | `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio` and `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG`, before process start |
| `metrics: false` | `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none` |
| `metrics: true` | Leave `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` unset. Metrics start when a metrics URL is set. |
| `metrics.exportIntervalMillis` | `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL`, milliseconds, before process start |
| `logs: false` | Unset `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER`, or set `none` |
| `logs: true` | `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp` |
| `logs.userPrompts` | `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp` and `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1` |
| `logs.toolContent` | `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp` and `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1` |
| `otel: false` | No endpoint, or `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` |

Set the hosted values after deploy:

```bash
agent-sdk secret set my-agent OTEL_SERVICE_NAME OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS
```

---

Source: /docs/guides/pagerduty.md

# PagerDuty agents

A PagerDuty agent wakes when an incident triggers, investigates it, and writes what it found back to
the incident. `pagerdutyChannel()` verifies PagerDuty's v3 webhooks and sends every later event for
that incident to the session that started the investigation.

## Investigate a new incident

When an incident triggers, the agent starts a turn with the incident's title, service, urgency, and
link.

```ts
// bot/channels/pagerduty.ts
import { defaultPagerDutyAuth, pagerdutyChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/pagerduty";

export default pagerdutyChannel({
  deliverReplies: true,
  onIncident: (ctx, event) => {
    if (event.eventType !== "incident.triggered") {
      return null;
    }
    return {
      // `auth` starts a model turn running as the event's PagerDuty actor.
      auth: defaultPagerDutyAuth(ctx),
      message: `Investigate PagerDuty incident #${event.incident.number}: ${event.incident.title}`,
      context: [`Service: ${event.incident.service?.summary ?? "unknown"}`],
    };
  },
});
```

With `deliverReplies: true`, the channel posts each reply as a note on the incident. It doesn't post
anything until it knows the agent's own PagerDuty user, because each note comes back as a webhook
event and would otherwise start another turn. Handlers you write in `events` replace the built-in
ones.

Hooks also get `ctx.pagerduty`, a REST client with the channel's credentials. Use the incident from
the event or channel state when you write, so the model can't choose the target.

```ts
onIncident: async (ctx, event) => {
  const incident = await ctx.pagerduty.getIncident(event.incident.id);
  // …
},
```

On Cursor hosting, declare PagerDuty's API host and the token:

```ts
// bot/agent.ts
import { defineAgent } from "@grok/agent-sdk";

export default defineAgent({
  hosting: {
    egressDomains: ["api.pagerduty.com"],
    secretNames: ["PAGERDUTY_TOKEN"],
  },
});
```

## Follow the incident in one session

People acknowledge, annotate, reassign, and resolve an incident while the agent investigates. Return
a dispatch for those events too, and each one reaches the session already working on the incident.

```ts
onIncident: (ctx, event) => {
  const followUps = ["incident.acknowledged", "incident.reassigned", "incident.resolved"];
  if (event.eventType !== "incident.triggered" && !followUps.includes(event.eventType)) {
    return null;
  }
  return {
    auth: defaultPagerDutyAuth(ctx),
    message: `${event.eventType} by ${ctx.agent?.summary ?? "PagerDuty"}`,
  };
},
onNote: (ctx, note) => {
  return {
    auth: defaultPagerDutyAuth(ctx),
    message: `Note on the incident: ${note.content}`,
  };
},
```

Add both to the same `pagerdutyChannel()` call. A re-trigger after a resolve is a new PagerDuty
incident, so it starts a new session. `ctx.incidentKey` carries the alert's dedup key, so the agent
can recall what it found the last time the same alert fired.

## Ignore your own actions

PagerDuty sends the agent's own changes back as webhook events, such as a note it posted or an
incident it resolved. The channel acknowledges those events without starting a turn, and the same
action by a person still arrives.

```ts
export default pagerdutyChannel({
  // Events caused by the agent's own PagerDuty user are skipped.
  // The user comes from, in order: selfUserIds, PAGERDUTY_USER_ID,
  // or the user PAGERDUTY_TOKEN acts as (GET /users/me).
  selfUserIds: ["PBOT001"],
  onIncident: (ctx) => ({ auth: defaultPagerDutyAuth(ctx) }),
});
```

A user-level API key or an OAuth user token acts as one user. An account-level key or an app token
acts as no user, so the channel uses the user whose email matches `PAGERDUTY_FROM_EMAIL`. A
read-only agent with no token sets `PAGERDUTY_USER_ID` instead. When none of these names a user, the
channel skips nothing.

## Events

Each hook receives one family of v3 events:

| Hook          | Events                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `onIncident`  | `incident.triggered`, `.acknowledged`, `.unacknowledged`, `.escalated`, `.reassigned`, `.delegated`, `.resolved`, `.reopened`, `.priority_updated`, `.incident_type.changed` |
| `onNote`      | `incident.annotated`                                                                                                                                                         |
| `onResponder` | `incident.responder.added`, `incident.responder.replied`                                                                                                                     |
| `onEvent`     | Everything else, such as status updates and workflow events                                                                                                                  |

Without `onIncident`, a triggered or reopened incident starts a turn. The channel acknowledges every
other event until you add its hook. Each hook returns `{ auth }`, `{ task }`, or `null`, as
[Handler results](/docs/reference/channels.md#handler-results) describes.

## Connect

Create a v3 webhook subscription in PagerDuty for the services the agent should respond to, and
point it at `https://<your-host>/<slug>/v1/channels/pagerduty`. Set the channel's secrets on the
deployment, or as environment variables locally.

| Variable                   | Used for                                                                                                               | Override                                 |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Verifying `X-PagerDuty-Signature`. On Cursor hosting, a delivery with a bad signature gets a `401`.                    | `webhookSecret: { secretName }`          |
| `PAGERDUTY_USER_ID`        | The agent's own PagerDuty user ID. Optional when `PAGERDUTY_TOKEN` names a user.                                       | `selfUserIds: [ids]` or `{ secretName }` |
| `PAGERDUTY_TOKEN`          | Reply notes, `ctx.pagerduty`, and finding the agent's user. Use a REST API key, or an OAuth token as `Bearer <token>`. | `token: { secretName }`                  |
| `PAGERDUTY_FROM_EMAIL`     | The `From` user for writes with an account-level key or app token.                                                     | `from: { secretName }`                   |
| `PAGERDUTY_API_BASE_URL`   | The REST host, such as `https://api.eu.pagerduty.com`. Defaults to `https://api.pagerduty.com`.                        | `apiBaseUrl`                             |

`createPagerDutyClient()` takes the same options for code outside the channel.

```bash
agent-sdk deploy --dir . --slug incident-responder
agent-sdk secret set incident-responder PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET PAGERDUTY_TOKEN
```

The next delivery picks up a new value without another deploy. Until the webhook secret is set, the
route accepts only loopback deliveries under `agent-sdk dev`.

### Several subscriptions

PagerDuty gives each webhook subscription its own signing secret. Put one secret on each line of
`PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`:

```text
<signing secret of subscription 1>
<signing secret of subscription 2>
```

A delivery passes when its signature matches any line. Set the value from that file:

```bash
agent-sdk secret set incident-responder PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET < pagerduty-webhook-secrets.txt
```

To rotate a secret, add the new one before PagerDuty signs with it, and remove the old one once
nothing signs with it.

## Test locally

`agent-sdk pagerduty replay` posts synthesized v3 deliveries for one incident to the running agent,
in order. Without `PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `agent-sdk dev` admits them unsigned from loopback.
With it set, replay signs them the way PagerDuty does.

```bash
agent-sdk dev &
agent-sdk pagerduty replay --events triggered,acknowledged,annotated,resolved \
  --comment "Rolled back the 09:30 deploy."
```

Each event joins the session the trigger started. Pass an incident ID to start another session,
`--dry-run` to print the bodies, or `--fixtures-dir fixtures/pagerduty` to save them as fixtures for
[evals](/docs/evals.md).

To post a delivery you saved from the webhook log, sign it:

```bash
export PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET=local-test-secret
agent-sdk dev &

body=fixtures/pagerduty/incident-triggered.json
signature=$(openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET" -hex < "$body" | awk '{print $NF}')
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/<slug>/v1/channels/pagerduty \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "x-pagerduty-signature: v1=$signature" \
  --data-binary @"$body"
```

## Related

- [Channels reference](/docs/reference/channels.md)
- [Webhooks and custom channels](/docs/guides/webhooks.md)
- [Evals](/docs/evals.md)
