Source: /docs/guides/slack.md

# Slack Agents

Agent SDK makes it easy to build agents that work in Slack.

A Slack agent wakes when someone mentions it, sends it a DM, or posts in a channel it watches. From
there, it keeps the conversation in one thread and can reply all at once, stream the answer live, or
decide for itself when to post updates. [Connect](#connect) sets up the Slack app.

## Answer a mention or DM

Mention the bot in a channel or send it a DM, and it will answer in a thread on that message. Any
follow-up in the same thread continues the conversation where it left off. All messages in one DM
share a session by default. Set `continuation: "slack.dmthread/v2"` to give each top-level DM its
own session and thread.

```ts
// bot/channels/slack.ts
import { slackChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/slack";

export default slackChannel({
  // Reads TRIAGE_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and TRIAGE_SLACK_APP_TOKEN, so two bots
  // on one host don't collide.
  envPrefix: "TRIAGE",
});
```

## Post one reply with a status chip

By default, Slack shows a status chip under the thread while the turn runs, with idle messages until
reasoning or tool activity gives it more to show. When the turn finishes, the chip disappears and
one complete reply lands in the thread.

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  reply: {
    mode: "post",
    status: {
      // First line of each reasoning block on the chip.
      reasoning: true,
      // Tool names as they start ("Running grep, glob...").
      tools: true,
      idle: ["Checking the request...", "Reviewing recent activity..."],
    },
  },
});
```

## Stream a live reply

In stream mode, the reply appears immediately and grows as the model writes. Slack shows its generic
"is working..." state until the stream ends, while optional reasoning and tool cards keep progress
inside the same message.

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  reply: {
    mode: "stream",
    // Thinking card inside the streamed message.
    reasoningCard: true,
    // One card per tool in that same message.
    toolCards: true,
  },
});
```

## Let the agent own every message

Use agentic mode when the agent should decide how to communicate as well as what to say. The bot
reacts to the parent message with eyes and shows a thinking chip, then the agent chooses when to
post progress and how to deliver the final reply.

`slack-communication` gives those posts a Slack-aware voice by default. Use `tone` to set the voice,
level of detail, formatting, and structure of updates.

```ts
// bot/extensions/slack.ts
import slackCommunication from "@grok/agent-sdk/extensions/slack-communication";

export default slackCommunication({
  tone: "Be concise but warm. Use bullets for evidence and end with the next action.",
});
```

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  // `post-update` writes mid-turn progress and the final reply.
  reply: { mode: "agentic" },
});
```

### Show steps as cards or as a checklist

The agent calls `post-card` to show one step of its work, such as "Scan the repo", with an `id`, a
`title`, a `status`, and optional `details`. Calling it again with the same `id` updates that card,
for example from `in_progress` to `complete`.

`cards` sets how Slack draws these steps:

| `cards`                             | What Slack shows                            | Use it when                                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `{ display: "timeline" }` (default) | A separate card in the thread for each step | One or two short steps                        |
| `{ display: "plan" }`               | One checklist for every step in the turn    | Several steps that readers track in one place |

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  reply: {
    mode: "agentic",
    cards: { display: "plan", title: "Release check" },
  },
});
```

- `title` is optional and can be up to 256 characters.
- `pending` only works when `display` is `"plan"`.

## Wake on a channel post

This example watches `#triage-alerts`, so any substantial top-level message starts a thread even
when nobody mentions the bot.

Mentions work in any channel the bot has joined. To listen without a mention, list between 1 and 10
channel IDs that start with `C` or `G`, plus optional `#name` entries for readability. On its own,
`"*"` watches thread replies in every joined channel but never wakes on top-level posts.

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  engagement: {
    channelPosts: {
      allow: ["C0123ABCDEF", "#triage-alerts"],
      posts: "top-level",
      debounceMs: 15_000,
    },
  },
  onChannelPost: async (_ctx, message) => {
    if (message.markdown.length <= 20) {
      return null;
    }
    // `{}` starts a model turn as the sender.
    return {};
  },
});
```

When you create the app, pass `--channel-posts` and invite the bot to every channel in the
allowlist. Add the `channels:read` scope when you use `#name` entries. On Cursor hosting,
`debounceMs` has no effect.

## Control who can message

By default, the agent doesn't reply to people outside your workspace, such as Slack Connect guests.
Set `blockExternals: false` only if those people should be able to use the agent.

Anyone in a thread can continue its session by default. To keep the conversation between the agent
and the person who started it, set `respondTo: "author"`.

```ts
export default slackChannel({
  policy: { blockExternals: false, respondTo: "author" },
});
```

## Events

Mentions and DMs wake the agent automatically. Declare `onAppMention` or `onDirectMessage` to filter
them. Like `onChannelPost`, each handler returns `{}` to start a turn or `null` to skip the message.
This handler only starts a turn for DMs that begin with `triage:`:

```ts
onDirectMessage: async (_ctx, message) => {
  if (!message.markdown.startsWith("triage:")) {
    return null;
  }
  return {};
},
```

## Call Slack from deterministic code via `ctx`

A hook can post a fixed acknowledgement before the model turn starts, using `ctx.thread.post()`,
`ctx.slack.channelId`, and `ctx.slack.threadTs`, while tools call the Slack Web API with
`ctx.host.slack.getClient()`.

```ts
onAppMention: async (ctx, message) => {
  if (message.markdown.trim() === "") {
    return null;
  }
  await ctx.thread.post("Looking at this now.");
  return {};
},
```

## Connect

```bash
agent-sdk login
agent-sdk slack create --dir .
agent-sdk slack doctor --prefix TRIAGE
agent-sdk serve --dir . --dev
```

After you sign in, `slack create` opens **Add Slack to this agent** in the browser and writes the
resulting tokens to `.env.local` without printing them. You can open the same wizard from
**Integrations** on [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents). `doctor`
catches missing credentials before you start the agent. The
[CLI reference](/docs/reference/cli.md#slack) covers each `slack` command.

If your workspace requires admin approval, keep `slack create` running and open the **Request
approval** link it prints. Installing from Deployed Agents doesn't send that request. After an admin
approves, select **Retry** in the **Add Slack** wizard there.

### Choose the bot scopes

A Cursor-managed app requests these bot scopes by default:

`app_mentions:read`, `assistant:write`, `channels:history`, `channels:read`, `chat:write`,
`files:read`, `files:write`, `groups:history`, `groups:read`, `im:history`, `im:read`, `im:write`,
`mpim:history`, `reactions:read`, `reactions:write`, `usergroups:read`, `users:read`,
`users:read.email`

To request a different list, set `botScopes` in `slack-manifest.json` at the root of the agent
project. The app then requests exactly that list:

```json
{
  "botScopes": [
    "app_mentions:read",
    "assistant:write",
    "channels:history",
    "chat:write",
    "groups:history",
    "im:history",
    "reactions:read",
    "pins:read"
  ]
}
```

Then run `agent-sdk slack create` again (add `--env prod` for the production app), and Slack updates
and reinstalls the app.

- The list must include `app_mentions:read`, `assistant:write`, `channels:history`, `chat:write`,
  `groups:history`, `im:history`, and `reactions:read`.
- Cursor rejects scopes in the Slack Marketplace forbidden families: `admin.*`, `identity.*`,
  `search:read*`, `triggers:*`, `apps_configuration:*`, and `workflow.steps:execute`.

The person who runs `slack create` grants Cursor three user scopes on their own account so it can
create and install the app, and `botScopes` doesn't change them.

If you already own the Slack app, run `agent-sdk slack init --manual --dir . --name "Triage"` and
follow the `bdk-setup-slack` skill for installation and tokens.

Source: /docs/guides/webhooks.md

# Webhook agents

A custom channel turns an event from another system into an agent
conversation and sends the result back to the system that started it.
Use one when the built-in [HTTP API](/docs/reference/http-api.md) doesn't
match the provider's payload, conversation key, or reply path.

A file at `bot/channels/<id>.ts` mounts its routes under
`/<slug>/v1/channels/<id>`.

## Receive a webhook and send the answer back

When a ticket system sends a new message, this route starts a turn and
answers right away. The agent keeps working after the HTTP request ends,
and its answer appears as a comment on the ticket.

```ts
// bot/channels/tickets.ts
import { defineChannel, POST } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels";
import { z } from "zod";
import { postTicketComment } from "../lib/tickets.js";

type TicketState = {
  ticketId: string;
};

export default defineChannel<TicketState>({
  state: { ticketId: "" },
  routes: [
    POST("/ticket", {
      description: "Answer a new ticket message",
      bodySchema: z.object({
        ticketId: z.string(),
        message: z.string(),
      }),
      handler: async (_request, { send, waitUntil, body }) => {
        waitUntil(
          send(body.message, {
            state: { ticketId: body.ticketId },
            title: `Ticket ${body.ticketId}`,
          })
        );
        return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
      },
    }),
  ],
  events: {
    async "message.completed"(event, channel) {
      if (event.data.finishReason === "tool_call" || event.data.text === "") {
        return;
      }
      await postTicketComment(channel.state.ticketId, event.data.text);
    },
  },
});
```

`postTicketComment` wraps the ticket provider's SDK. The write lives in
the event handler, so the webhook request doesn't stay open while the
model works.

On Cursor hosting, the caller always gets an empty `202` response, and
the platform ignores whatever your handler returns. Send results and
failures back through the provider's API instead. See
[Route responses](/docs/reference/channels.md#route-responses).

## Keep one conversation per ticket

Without a conversation key, every delivery creates a new session. Pass
the ticket ID as the `continuationToken`, so every message on one
ticket resumes the same conversation.

```ts
waitUntil(
  send(body.message, {
    continuationToken: `ticket:${body.ticketId}`,
    state: { ticketId: body.ticketId },
    title: `Ticket ${body.ticketId}`,
  })
);
```

## Keep one hosted session per thread

On Cursor hosting, each request to a custom route starts a new session,
even when the handler passes the same `continuationToken`. To join
requests, the sender or a small relay in front of the deployment adds
the same `X-BDK-Session-Key` value to each one, and those requests run
in one session in arrival order.

```bash
curl -X POST "$AGENT_ALIAS_URL/v1/channels/tickets/ticket" \
  -H "X-Agent-Alias-Token: $AGENT_ALIAS_TOKEN" \
  -H "X-BDK-Session-Key: ticket:ENG-142" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ticketId":"ENG-142","message":"CSV export returns 500"}'
```

Hosting stores the value with the request, so don't put secrets or
personal data in it.
[Hosted session keys](/docs/reference/channels.md#hosted-session-keys)
lists the auth, format, and retry rules.

## Prepare evidence before the turn

Webhook payloads often carry little more than an object ID. This
handler fetches the full ticket with a server tool and writes it to
`ticket.json`, so the model starts from a fixed snapshot.

```ts
handler: async (_request, { callTool, send, waitUntil, body }) => {
  const prepared = await callTool("prepare_ticket", {
    ticketId: body.ticketId,
  });
  if (prepared.isError) {
    await postTicketComment(
      body.ticketId,
      "I couldn't load this ticket, so I didn't draft a reply."
    );
    return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
  }

  waitUntil(
    send("Read ticket.json, then draft the reply.", {
      continuationToken: `ticket:${body.ticketId}`,
      state: { ticketId: body.ticketId },
      workspaceFiles: {
        "ticket.json": JSON.stringify(prepared.result, null, 2) ?? "null",
      },
    })
  );
  return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
},
```

The `message.completed` handler from the first example still delivers
the answer.

## Validate payloads with Zod

The route validates the request and passes the handler a typed `body`
or `query`. `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` routes need a Zod `bodySchema`,
and `GET` routes need a `querySchema`. Use `z.unknown()` for a variable
payload that your own parser narrows.

## Use handler context

Await `send` instead of passing it to `waitUntil` when later handler
code needs the session, for example to call
`session.waitForCompletion()`.
[Handler arguments](/docs/reference/channels.md#handler-arguments) lists
every helper.

## Protect public webhooks

Custom routes accept direct loopback requests by default and reject
forwarded ones, so a tunnel or reverse proxy can't quietly make a local
endpoint public. Under `--dev`, a provider channel with no webhook
secret (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or PagerDuty) accepts only local
requests, so set that secret in the provider and in your shell before
you test through a tunnel.

Use `bearerAuth()` when the sender can attach an authorization header.
Webhook providers often can't attach the agent alias token, so
`publicEndpoint()` lets a custom channel skip it on Cursor hosting.
That opens the route to every caller, so verify the provider's
signature before you start a turn or call a tool.

```ts
import { defineChannel, POST, publicEndpoint } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels";
import { z } from "zod";
import { verifyProviderSignature } from "../lib/tickets.js";

export default defineChannel({
  auth: [publicEndpoint()],
  routes: [
    POST("/", {
      description: "Signed ticket webhook",
      bodySchema: z.unknown(),
      handler: async request => {
        const rawBody = await request.text();
        const signature = request.headers.get("x-provider-signature");
        if (!verifyProviderSignature(rawBody, signature)) {
          return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
        }

        // Parse and dispatch only after the signature passes.
        return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
      },
    }),
  ],
});
```

With `publicEndpoint()`, the handler drops a badly signed delivery
silently. If the provider sends a shared secret header or signs the raw
body with HMAC-SHA256, use `sharedSecretAuth()` or
`hmacSignatureAuth()` instead. Hosting checks those policies before the
handler runs and answers a bad delivery with `401`.

`publicEndpoint()` opens only this channel's routes, and the built-in
session and tool APIs stay private. See
[Auth policies](/docs/reference/channels.md#auth-policies).

## Test locally

Run the agent with `--dev` and post the payload the provider will send.
The session appears in the playground while the reply goes out.

```text
agent-sdk serve --dir . --dev

curl -sS -X POST \
  http://127.0.0.1:3000/<slug>/v1/channels/tickets/ticket \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ticketId":"ENG-142","message":"CSV export returns 500"}'
```

Keep sample payloads under `fixtures/` and pass them with
`--data-binary @fixtures/<event>.json`.

- [Channels reference](/docs/reference/channels.md)
- [Review and triage templates](/docs/templates/reviews.md), including a
  signed tracker webhook

# Hillclimbing

Hillclimbing improves an agent one measured change at a time. Hold the inputs fixed, change one
thing, and keep it only when the same run gets better without moving the behavior you froze.

A coding agent in your checkout can run this loop by following the `bdk-hillclimb` skill.

## Run one measured round

First agree on the agent, one to three fixed inputs, the metric to improve, and the behavior that
must not change, such as the output shape, side effects, and existing evals.

Then run one round:

1. Run the agent the way a user would, on saved or local inputs, without deploying or posting live.
2. Read the trajectory and name the main failure in one sentence.
3. Change one lever.
4. Rerun the same fixtures.
5. Compare correctness, efficiency, and contract fit.
6. Keep, revert, or narrow the change.

Don't swap a fixture mid-round, or the comparison means nothing.

## Choose the smallest lever

Start with the earliest place that can remove the failure. Prepare evidence on the host before the
turn, then change the shape of that evidence, then the instructions or skills, then remove or gate
tools that invite wandering, and change the framework only when the agent can't express the fix.

Fixing the host or evidence often improves quality and latency together, because the model searches
less for ground truth.

## Match the fix to the failure

When the agent picks the wrong tool, such as a PR reviewer that calls `approve_pr` before
`inspect_pr`, pin one PR and tighten only the instruction that owns that decision, so you know which
edit fixed it.

```ts
t.calledTool("inspect_pr");
t.notCalledTool("approve_pr");
```

When a run wanders or runs long, it often repeats reads or makes the model find evidence the host
already has. Move that preparation ahead of the turn, and keep the change only if the answer still
finds the same issue.

```text
before: 14 tool calls, 92 seconds, 6 repeated reads
after:   5 tool calls, 31 seconds, 0 repeated reads
```

When the answer is weak, freeze the public shape, compare both runs against known-good findings, and
edit the instruction or skill that owns the missing judgment.

```text
fixture: saved checkout PR diff
success: report both gold findings with file paths
freeze:  findings JSON shape; no review post; existing smoke evals
```

## Lock every kept win

Each kept change needs an eval that would have failed before it, such as a tool-choice assertion, a
`maxToolCalls` bound, an output-shape check, or a quality score.

```bash
agent-sdk eval --dir . --tag smoke
```

Don't loosen an existing eval so that a new change passes. If an older eval starts failing, the
change broke something that used to work, and you should fix the change instead.

---

Source: /docs/index.md

# Agent SDK

Agent SDK lets you define, test, evaluate, and deploy agents as code. It uses the Cursor SDK harness
that powers Bugbot, Security Review, Approval Bot, and Rollouts.

An Agent's behavior is defined in a folder of Markdown and TypeScript that combines deterministic
code with model judgment. Agent SDK makes it easy to build useful agents, with APIs to interact on
Slack, pull requests, issue trackers, Cursor, and the other places where you get work done.

After you deploy an agent, open [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents) to
manage it.

## Get Started with your Coding Agent

Paste this prompt into your coding agent. It installs the CLI, asks what your agent is for, and
scaffolds a first project from the Markdown version of these docs.

```text
Set up my first Agent SDK project.

Read https://cursor.com/docs/agent-sdk.md first. Every page under
https://cursor.com/docs/agent-sdk/ is also available as Markdown when you
add .md to its URL.

1. Check that Node is 22.13 or newer, then run:
   npm install --global @grok/agent-sdk
2. Read the docs index that ships with the package:
   "$(npm root -g)/@grok/agent-sdk/dist/docs/llms.txt"
3. Run agent-sdk login, and wait while I finish the browser sign-in.
4. Ask me what the agent should do and where people will reach it. Then
   follow the bdk-create-agent skill at
   "$(npm root -g)/@grok/agent-sdk/skills/create-agent/SKILL.md"
   to scaffold the project with agent-sdk init.
5. Run agent-sdk validate --dir . and one agent-sdk run turn, then show me
   the reply.
```

## Why Agent SDK

Your instructions, tools, and evals are files you review, test, and version like the rest of your
code. You write the instructions and tools, and Cursor runs the model loop that calls them.

## When to use Agent SDK

|                    | Cursor Automations                            | Grok Bot                                                        | Agent SDK                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **You define**     | A prompt, model, and trigger in the dashboard | Instructions, skills, and connected tools in the app            | A versioned Markdown and TypeScript project                                                        |
| **Where it runs**  | Cursor-managed                                | Cursor-managed                                                  | Cursor-managed hosting or your infrastructure                                                      |
| **Choose it when** | The job fits a schedule or event trigger      | You want to configure and talk to an agent without writing code | You want code around model judgment that your team can version control, review, test and hillclimb |

## Get started

Install `@grok/agent-sdk`, then scaffold and run a project. The package was `@cursor/bdk` before.

```bash
npm install --global @grok/agent-sdk
agent-sdk init ./my-bot
cd my-bot
agent-sdk dev
```

[Project layout](/docs/reference/project-layout.md) explains every folder under `bot/`.

## Next steps

- [Build your first PR reviewer agent](/docs/quickstart.md) step by step.
- Start from a [review or triage template](/docs/templates/reviews.md) or the
  [owners-policy approver](/docs/templates/agentic-owners.md).
- [Convert a Cursor Automation](/docs/guides/convert-automation.md) into an Agent SDK project.
- [Build agents with agents](/docs/building-with-agents.md) using a coding agent.
- Look up commands in the [CLI reference](/docs/reference/cli.md) and deployed-agent roles in
  [Access](/docs/reference/access.md).

# Build a PR reviewer with Agent SDK

You'll build a reviewer that rates each pull request as `trivial`, `moderate`, or `large`, then approves safe changes or asks for a human review.

When it's deployed, you'll manage it in [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents).

## Build it with a coding agent

Paste this prompt into your coding agent to build the reviewer from this page. The sections after
it walk through the same steps by hand.

```text
Build the PR reviewer from https://cursor.com/docs/agent-sdk/quickstart.md
in ./pr-reviewer. Fetch that page and follow each step in order.

- If agent-sdk isn't on PATH, install it with
  npm install --global @grok/agent-sdk. Wait while I finish agent-sdk login.
- Use the code from the page as written. Ask me for a GitHub repository and
  a pull request I didn't author, and use them in place of acme/checkout#42.
- Run both tool-call checks, and confirm the complexity each one reports.
- Ask me before any step that posts a review on GitHub. Skip the deploy step.

Finish with agent-sdk validate --dir . and the project's TypeScript check,
then tell me what passed.
```

## Prerequisites

You need Node 22.13 or newer and a Cursor login for model turns:

```bash
npm install -g @grok/agent-sdk
agent-sdk login
```

## Create and run the project

```bash
agent-sdk init ./pr-reviewer
cd pr-reviewer
agent-sdk dev
```

In a second terminal, confirm the agent replies:

```bash
agent-sdk run --dir . --message "Introduce yourself in one sentence."
```

## Add review instructions

Replace `bot/instructions.md`:

```md
# PR reviewer

Call `inspect_pr` before you judge a pull request, then act on the
complexity it reports:

- `trivial`: approve with `submit_review` if the diff matches the title
  and nothing looks risky.
- `moderate`: approve only when you understand every patch and see no
  risk. Otherwise request a human review and name the files that worry you.
- `large`: request a human review right away and point the reviewer at
  the biggest files.

Never approve a draft. End with one sentence that gives the verdict and why.
```

## Share the URL parser

Both tools parse a pull request URL, so put the parser in `bot/lib/github.ts`, where Agent SDK doesn't look for tools.

```ts
export function parsePrUrl(prUrl: string) {
  const [owner, repo, pulls, number] = new URL(prUrl).pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean);
  const pull_number = Number.parseInt(number ?? "", 10);
  if (pulls !== "pull" || owner === undefined || repo === undefined || Number.isNaN(pull_number)) {
    throw new Error(`Not a pull request URL: ${prUrl}`);
  }
  return { owner, repo, pull_number };
}
```

## Add the inspect tool

Create `bot/tools/inspect_pr.ts`. It skips patches on a large pull request and caps the rest at 3,000 characters.

```ts
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";
import { parsePrUrl } from "../lib/github.js";

function rateComplexity(linesChanged: number, changedFiles: number) {
  if (linesChanged <= 25 && changedFiles <= 2) {
    return "trivial";
  }
  if (linesChanged <= 400 && changedFiles <= 15) {
    return "moderate";
  }
  return "large";
}

export default defineTool({
  description: "Fetch a pull request's title, patches, and complexity.",
  inputSchema: z.object({ prUrl: z.string().describe("GitHub pull request URL") }),
  async execute({ prUrl }, ctx) {
    const pull = parsePrUrl(prUrl);
    const octokit = await ctx.host.github.getOctokit();
    const { data: pr } = await octokit.rest.pulls.get(pull);
    const { data: files } = await octokit.rest.pulls.listFiles({ ...pull, per_page: 100 });
    const complexity = rateComplexity(pr.additions + pr.deletions, pr.changed_files);

    return {
      title: pr.title,
      draft: pr.draft ?? false,
      complexity,
      files: files.map((file) => ({
        path: file.filename,
        additions: file.additions,
        deletions: file.deletions,
        patch: complexity === "large" ? undefined : file.patch?.slice(0, 3000),
      })),
    };
  },
});
```

## Verify complexity classification

Call the tool without a model turn:

```bash
# Expect "complexity": "trivial"
agent-sdk tool call inspect_pr --dir . --input '{"prUrl":"https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/35623"}'

# Expect "complexity": "large" and no patch fields
agent-sdk tool call inspect_pr --dir . --input '{"prUrl":"https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/25229"}'
```

## Add the review tool

Create `bot/tools/submit_review.ts`:

```ts
import { defineTool } from "@grok/agent-sdk/tools";
import { z } from "zod";
import { parsePrUrl } from "../lib/github.js";

export default defineTool({
  description: "Approve the pull request, or comment asking for a human review.",
  inputSchema: z.object({
    prUrl: z.string().describe("GitHub pull request URL"),
    verdict: z.enum(["approve", "request_human_review"]),
    summary: z.string().describe("One or two sentences on why."),
  }),
  async execute({ prUrl, verdict, summary }, ctx) {
    const approve = verdict === "approve";
    const octokit = await ctx.host.github.getOctokit();
    await octokit.rest.pulls.createReview({
      ...parsePrUrl(prUrl),
      event: approve ? "APPROVE" : "COMMENT",
      body: approve ? summary : `Human review needed. ${summary}`,
    });
    return { posted: true, verdict };
  },
});
```

You need GitHub write access and a pull request you didn't author.

## Review a pull request

```bash
agent-sdk run --dir . --message "Review https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42"
```

Confirm `inspect_pr` runs before `submit_review`, then check the review on GitHub.

## Trigger reviews from GitHub

Create `bot/channels/github.ts`:

```ts
import { defaultGitHubAuth, githubChannel } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels/github";

const REVIEW_ACTIONS = new Set(["opened", "reopened", "ready_for_review"]);

export default githubChannel({
  botName: "agent-sdk-pr-reviewer",
  cursorAccount: { repos: ["acme/checkout"] },
  onPullRequest: (ctx, pr) => {
    if (!REVIEW_ACTIONS.has(pr.action) || pr.draft) {
      return null;
    }

    return {
      auth: defaultGitHubAuth(ctx),
      title: `Review ${ctx.repository.fullName}#${pr.number}`,
      context: [`Review ${pr.url}.`],
    };
  },
});
```

With `agent-sdk dev` running, replay an open pull request. Pull access is enough:

```bash
agent-sdk github replay https://github.com/acme/checkout/pull/42 --dir . --action opened
```

Open the playground and confirm `Review acme/checkout#42` shows both tool calls and the verdict.

## Deploy the reviewer

Follow [Deployment](/docs/deployment.md) to run `agent-sdk deploy`, then manage the reviewer in [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents).

## Where to go next

- Turn these two PRs into regression checks with [Evals](/docs/evals.md).
- Read about typed tools in [Tools](/docs/reference/tools.md).
- Set up fixtures and forwarding with the [GitHub guide](/docs/guides/github.md).

Source: /docs/reference/access.md

# Access

[Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents) calls the three access levels Viewer, Editor, and Owner, and the API calls them `viewer`, `deployer`, and `admin`. `admin` is Owner, and a write also accepts `owner` for that role and `editor` for Editor.

| Dashboard | API value | What it allows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Viewer | `viewer` | Open the bot |
| Editor | `deployer` | Deploy, stop, and restart |
| Owner | `admin` | Editor, plus secrets and who else has access |

A new deploy gives the person who deployed it Owner and the team that owns the bot Viewer. Deploying that bot again does not change who has access. A team that already has access keeps it.

A deploy from a service account, such as CI, gives Owner to the person who created that account. The service account is not an Owner. If the account has no creating person, the team is Viewer and a team Admin can manage the bot.

A team Admin can manage every bot that team owns, including a bot the team can only view. The same person cannot manage a bot another team published, including a catalog bot installed into their team.

An Owner changes who has access in [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents).

---

Source: /docs/reference/agent-config.md

# Agent config

`bot/agent.ts` default-exports `defineAgent(config)`, which sets the model
that runs the agent and the defaults for a local run. Every field is optional on
the root agent.

```ts
import { defineAgent } from "@grok/agent-sdk";

export default defineAgent({
  model: {
    id: "grok-4.5",
    params: [
      { id: "effort", value: "high" },
      { id: "fast", value: "true" },
    ],
  }, // optional; this is the default
});
```

## Agent fields

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | string or `{ id, params }` | Cursor model for turns. Defaults to `grok-4.5` with `effort=high` and `fast=true`. Subagents omit it to inherit. |
| `name` | string | Display name. Defaults to the package or directory name. |
| `description` | string | What the agent is for. Required on subagents, where the parent model reads it to decide when to delegate. |
| `instructions` | string | Inline instructions for subagents and generated configs. Prefer `instructions.md`. |
| `local` | `{ cwd?, workspaceDir?, sandbox? }` | Defaults for a local run. See [Local options](#local-options). |
| `hosting` | `{ egressDomains?, secretNames? }` | The egress allowlist and expected secret names that `agent-sdk deploy` reads. Mounted [extensions](/docs/reference/extensions.md#build-an-extension) add their own. |
| `concurrency` | `{ maxRunningTurns? }` | Agent-wide limit on concurrent turns. See [Concurrency](#concurrency). |
| `builtinTools` | `{ reminders? }` | Opt-in tools that Agent SDK provides. See [Built-in tools](#built-in-tools). |
| `tools` | `ToolName[]` | Allowlist of built-in tools. Omit it for the full standard toolset. See [Harness tools](#harness-tools). |
| `fs` | `FileSystem` or `(ctx) => FileSystem` | Custom file tree for the session. `root` is the deprecated name. See [Custom filesystem](#custom-filesystem). |
| `skills` | `false` or `(ctx) => FileSystem` | Replaces the skills tree mounted at `/agent/skills`, or turns that mount off. |

The `persistent` field was removed. Discovery rejects a config that still sets it, and the error is `persistent was removed. Delete it from defineAgent.`, so `validate`, `dev`, and `deploy` fail until you delete the field. A deployment that is already running keeps serving until you stop or delete it.

## Model

Effort and speed are params, not id suffixes, so Agent SDK rejects an id like
`grok-4.5-fast`. Use the object form shown above to set params, or a plain
string when you don't need any:

```ts
model: "composer-2.5",
```

## Local options

`local.workspaceDir` points every session at one shared working directory, for
agents that work inside an existing checkout. It takes precedence over `cwd`,
and a per-send `workspaceDir` wins over both. Sessions share that tree, so one
turn's files are visible to the next.

`local.sandbox` runs the agent inside Cursor's local sandbox. It's off by
default, so shell commands auto-approve and inherit the serve process
environment, including the host's credentials. Turn it on when turns read
untrusted input, such as webhook payloads, PR diffs, or inbound chat. The
sandbox limits the tools themselves, so an injected prompt can't talk the model
past it.

Agent SDK runs the file tools (`read`, `edit`, `delete`, `grep`, `glob`, `ls`)
in the serve process, outside the sandbox. With `local.sandbox` on, they refuse
a path outside the session workspace with `Path is outside the workspace`. With
it off, they can reach any path the serve process can.

### Local cwd

`local.cwd` sets the parent directory for local session workspaces. Each
session uses `<cwd>/<sessionId>` unless a per-send `workspaceDir` overrides it.

Session workspaces are real Cursor project directories, so the local agent reads
`AGENTS.md` and `.cursor` config from every ancestor directory. When you omit
`cwd` and the agent sits inside another git repo, such as a monorepo package,
Agent SDK uses a per-project directory under `~/.cache` instead, so the
enclosing checkout's rules, skills, and MCP servers stay out of the turn. An
agent at its own git root keeps its workspaces inside the project. Point `cwd`
at a checkout only when the agent should inherit that tree.

## Custom filesystem

`fs` is mounted at `/`, and Agent SDK mounts `/tmp` and `/agent/skills` over it. Set `fs` or the deprecated `root`, not both. A tree that already has `/agent/skills` fails session start unless `skills` is `false`.

## Harness tools

Use `tools` to limit which built-in Cursor tools the model can call.
When you set it, the model gets only the tools you list. An empty list turns
off every built-in tool, and new platform tools stay off until you add them.

```ts
export default defineAgent({
  model: "composer-2.5",
  // Read-only triage: no shell, no edits, no subagents.
  tools: ["read", "grep", "glob", "ls"],
});
```

Agent SDK always adds `"mcp"` to a configured allowlist, because the server
tools in `bot/tools/` reach the model over MCP. With `local.sandbox` on, MCP
tool calls fail closed. An enclosing checkout can also add MCP servers, as
[Local cwd](#local-cwd) explains.

Use the Cursor SDK's public tool names, such as `"shell"`, `"read"`,
`"edit"`, `"grep"`, `"glob"`, `"ls"`, and `"task"`. An unknown name fails the
turn with a `ConfigurationError`, and `"SemanticSearch"` or `"semSearch"`
fails validation.

Two names have broader effects:

- `"shell"` also grants shell input. Tools with `execution: "agent"` need it
  to run their scripts, and discovery warns when your allowlist blocks them.
- `"task"` lets the root agent start subagents. Each subagent keeps its own
  toolset.

The allowlist doesn't isolate the serve host, so pair it with `local.sandbox`
for untrusted input.

## Migrate off semantic search

Semantic search is removed, and `agent-sdk validate` reports
`Semantic search has been removed. Use Grep.` while a project still uses it.
[A turn fails or misbehaves](/docs/troubleshooting.md#a-turn-fails-or-misbehaves) lists what to
delete and what to use instead.

## Concurrency

`concurrency.maxRunningTurns` caps how many model turns run at once across the agent's sessions. It takes a positive integer up to 200. Omit it for no limit.

When every slot is busy, a new turn queues in arrival order instead of failing. The stream records a `turn.queued` event with the queue
position, `GET /v1/sessions` reports `queued: true`, and the turn starts as
soon as a slot frees.

A queued turn still counts as running. A follow-up preempts it, and a direct
write-effect tool call gets `409 session_busy`.

```ts
export default defineAgent({
  concurrency: { maxRunningTurns: 3 },
});
```

## Built-in tools

`builtinTools` opts into tools that Agent SDK provides. They behave like your
own server tools in turns, direct calls, `info`, and the playground. A tool you
write with the same name wins, with a warning.

`builtinTools: { reminders: true }` adds `reminders_create`, `reminders_list`,
and `reminders_cancel`, bound to the current conversation. A session without a
continuation key can't set reminders. See
[Schedules and reminders](/docs/reference/schedules.md#reminders).

## Serve programmatically

`serve(dirOrProject, options)` embeds the server in your own process:

```ts
import { serve } from "@grok/agent-sdk";

const handle = await serve("./my-agent", {
  port: 3000,
});
console.log(`listening on ${handle.url}`);
// handle.callTool(...), handle.dispatchSchedule("heartbeat"),
// handle.createReminder(...), handle.agents, await handle.close()
```

`handle.agents` lists each mount as `{ slug, url, info }`. `handle.project` is
deprecated.

`serve()` takes the same host settings as the [CLI](/docs/reference/cli.md) `serve` flags,
plus `discovery` for project-loading options and `mode: "single" | "multi"`.
Pass `apiKey`, or sign in the same way as the CLI, as
[Environment variables](/docs/reference/cli.md#environment-variables) describes.

## Inspect a project in tests

`loadProject(dir)` reads one project without serving it. Its `info` matches the
`GET /v1/info` body.

```ts
import { loadProject } from "@grok/agent-sdk";

const { info } = await loadProject("./my-agent", { strict: true });
expect(info.tools.map((t) => t.name)).toContain("inspect_pr");
```

`loadProject` throws `ProjectLoadError` when discovery reports an error, and
`{ strict: true }` makes it throw on a warning too. `error.diagnostics` lists
the findings, and each `path` is relative to the project directory. `serve`
accepts the loaded project or a directory path.

## Related

- [Instructions](/docs/reference/instructions.md)
- [Sessions](/docs/reference/sessions.md)

---

Source: /docs/reference/artifacts.md

# Artifacts

Artifacts are durable outputs such as reviewed pull requests or
reports. Records persist across sessions, update by key, and can be
listed, streamed, or downloaded.

## Artifact kinds

Declare kinds in `bot/artifacts.ts`:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { defineArtifacts } from "@grok/agent-sdk/artifacts";

export default defineArtifacts({
  kinds: {
    "reviewed-pr": {
      description: "A pull request this agent reviewed.",
      schema: z.object({ url: z.string(), verdict: z.string() }),
    },
  },
  agentTool: true,
});
```

| Option | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `kinds` | Kind names, each with a non-empty `description` and optional Zod `schema` |
| `agentTool` | Expose `tag_artifact` to the model. Requires at least one declared kind |
| `max` | Retention cap, default `1000`. Only local and self-hosted servers evict, oldest-updated first |

With declared kinds, `tag` rejects any other kind, and without them it accepts any kind name and defaults an omitted kind to `"artifact"`. `tag` stores `data` as the kind's schema parsed it, with defaults and coercions applied.

## Tag artifacts from host code

Host code gets an `ArtifactsApi` with `tag` and `list`:

```ts
await ctx.artifacts.tag({
  kind: "reviewed-pr",
  key: prUrl,
  title: `Reviewed ${prUrl}`,
  data: { url: prUrl, verdict: "approve" },
});
```

`tag` returns an `ArtifactRecord`.

| Field | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | Declared or free-form kind |
| `data` | Required JSON data, validated by the kind's schema |
| `key` | Optional upsert key, unique across the agent and all kinds |
| `title` | Optional display title |
| `sessionId`, `turnId` | Optional session or turn attribution |
| `source` | `"host"` or `"model"`. `tag` defaults to `"host"` |
| `contents` | Tag only. String or bytes served by the content route |
| `contentType` | Tag only. MIME type for `contents` |
| `id` | Record only. Stable ID derived from `key`, or a generated ID |
| `content` | Record only. `{ size, contentType? }` metadata |
| `createdAt`, `updatedAt` | Record only. ISO-8601 timestamps |

Tool, hook, and channel-event contexts are session-bound and fill
`sessionId` and the current `turnId`. Channel routes, channel
`onStart`, schedules, and reminders get an unbound API, so pass
`sessionId` to attribute an artifact.

Re-tagging a key without `contents` keeps its payload unless
`sessionId` changes.

## Expose `tag_artifact` to the model

With `agentTool: true`, the model gets a generated `tag_artifact` tool
that accepts the declared kinds and validates data with their schemas.
Kind descriptions tell the model what each kind is for. An authored
`tag_artifact` tool takes precedence.

## List artifacts

`list({ kind?, sessionId? })` returns matching records, newest update
first. HTTP callers use the
[artifact routes](/docs/reference/http-api.md#list-and-download-artifacts) to list
and download.

## Stream artifact tags

Tagging with a `sessionId` emits
[`artifact.tagged`](/docs/reference/sessions.md#stream-events) on that session with
`id`, `kind`, `key`, `title`, `data`, and `source`.

---

Source: /docs/reference/channels.md

# Channels

A channel connects an external surface to agent sessions. A file at `bot/channels/<id>.ts` defines channel `<id>` and mounts its routes under `/v1/channels/<id>`, and the built-in HTTP channel serves the [HTTP API](/docs/reference/http-api.md) routes and is always available.

## Define a custom channel

Use `defineChannel` with one or more typed routes:

```ts
import { defineChannel, POST } from "@grok/agent-sdk/channels";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineChannel({
  routes: [
    POST("/review", {
      description: "Review a pull request on this channel",
      bodySchema: z.object({
        prUrl: z.string().url(),
      }),
      handler: async (_request, { send, waitUntil, body }) => {
        waitUntil(
          send(`Review ${body.prUrl}`, {
            continuationToken: `pr:${body.prUrl}`,
          })
        );
        return new Response(null, { status: 202 });
      },
    }),
  ],
});
```

This route is `POST /v1/channels/<id>/review`. Calls for the same pull request
pass the same [continuation token](/docs/reference/sessions.md#session-identifiers), so they
share one conversation.

## Route responses

On Cursor hosting, the deployment
answers every custom route with an empty `202 Accepted` as soon as the request
arrives, then runs the handler. The caller never sees the handler's `Response`,
so a route can't return a session ID, a result, or an error status. A request
that fails the alias token, `sharedSecretAuth`, or `hmacSignatureAuth` check
still gets `401`.

Deliver results through [`events`](#events) handlers, a callback to the sender,
or a tool the turn calls. Local `serve` returns the handler's response, so
return `new Response(null, { status: 202 })` to match hosting.

## Route verbs and schemas

Route paths must begin with `/`.

`GET` requires a `querySchema`.

`POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` require a `bodySchema`. They also accept a `querySchema`.

`DELETE` takes a `bodySchema`, a `querySchema`, either, or neither.

Plain JSON Schema objects don't type-check, so use `z.object({})` or
`z.unknown()` for an open surface. The host validates input before the handler
runs, and declared schemas appear in `GET /v1/info` for the playground and
slash commands.

## Handler arguments

A handler receives the Fetch `Request` and these arguments:

| Member | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `send(message, options?)` | Start or resume a session on this channel |
| `getSession(sessionId)` | This channel's session, or `null` |
| `receive(channel, input)` | Hand work to another channel |
| `callTool(name, input, options?)` | [Call a server tool](/docs/reference/tools.md#call-a-tool-without-a-model-turn) without a model turn |
| `body`, `query`, `params` | Validated inputs and `:param` path segments |
| `auth` | The `AuthContext` from the route's auth chain |
| `requestIp` | The TCP peer address, or `null` |
| `host` | Host services such as MCP, storage, telemetry, and reminders |
| `waitUntil(promise)` | Keep work running after the handler returns |
| `sessionUrls(request, sessionId)` | Playground and trace URLs for a session |
| `artifacts` | List or tag [artifacts](/docs/reference/artifacts.md) |

### `send` options

| Option | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `continuationToken` | Channel-local key that resumes its session, or creates one when new |
| `admission` | `"preempt"` (the default) interrupts a busy turn. `"coalesce"` queues behind it |
| `workspaceFiles` | Relative files to add before the next turn |
| `workspaceDir` | Absolute local working directory |
| `auth` | Session principal. Defaults to the request principal |
| `state` | Starting channel state for a new session |
| `title`, `purpose`, `dryRun`, `asOf` | Set up a new session, as in the [`POST /v1/session` body](/docs/reference/http-api.md#start-a-session) |
| `deliveryId` | Names this send on the session's [events](/docs/reference/sessions.md#track-which-follow-up-reached-the-agent), up to 256 characters. Defaults to a fresh `dlv_…` ID |

`send` returns a `ChannelSession` with `id`, the current `continuationToken`,
`isNew`, and `coalesced: true` for a coalesced call. On Cursor hosting, it
returns the ID before the session exists.

## Events

The `events` map subscribes the channel to stream events for its sessions. Keys
are types from the [event vocabulary](/docs/reference/sessions.md#stream-events), or `"*"`.
Each handler receives `(event, channel, ctx)` with `channel.state`, session
info, and host services, so it can post progress and replies. `state` on the
channel definition is each new session's starting JSON, unless a route passes
`state` to `send`, and handlers update it through `channel.state`.

## Start and stop a channel

`onStart(args)` runs when the channel mounts, and `onStop()` runs when the host
stops. Besides the route helpers, `onStart` receives
`emitAssistantMessage(sessionId, text)`, which appends assistant text without a
model turn, and `hasContinuationSession`, `isContinuationBusy`, and
`interruptContinuation`, which check or stop the session behind a token.

## Auth policies

Every route runs the channel's `auth` array, which defaults to `[localDevStrict()]`. The first policy to return an `AuthContext` admits the request, and if every policy returns `null`, the route answers `401`.

| Policy | Admits |
| --- | --- |
| `localDevStrict()` | Direct loopback requests with a loopback hostname and no forwarding headers |
| `localDev()` | The same, with any hostname |
| `loopbackOnly()` | Any loopback peer, including relays that add forwarding headers |
| `bearerAuth(tokenOrVerify)` | A matching bearer token, or one the verifier accepts |
| `sharedSecretAuth({ header, secret })` | A header that matches the named secret |
| `hmacSignatureAuth({ header, secret, prefix?, separator? })` | A hex HMAC-SHA256 signature of the raw body under the named secret, or any of several signatures split by `separator`. The secret can hold up to 32 values, one per line, and any of them verifies |
| `allowAll()` | Every caller, as an anonymous principal |
| `publicEndpoint()` | Every caller, with no alias token on hosting. The handler must verify the provider's signature |

Use `allowAll()` only for a public surface or one protected upstream. `publicEndpoint()` applies only to custom channel routes and doesn't
open the built-in session or tool API.

The admitted `AuthContext` becomes the request principal, which
[owns the sessions it creates](/docs/reference/sessions.md#session-contents).

On a channel without its own `auth`, `--bearer-token` swaps the default for
`bearerAuth(...)` and `--allow-anonymous` swaps it for `allowAll()`.

## Prebuilt channels

Import each one from `@grok/agent-sdk/channels/<name>`.

| Function | Details |
| --- | --- |
| `slackChannel()` | [Slack](/docs/guides/slack.md) |
| `githubChannel()` | [GitHub](/docs/guides/github.md) |
| `gitlabChannel()` | [GitLab](/docs/guides/gitlab.md) |
| `bitbucketChannel()` | [Bitbucket](/docs/guides/bitbucket.md) |
| `pagerdutyChannel()` | [PagerDuty](/docs/guides/pagerduty.md) |
| `deploymentsChannel()` | Deployment events filtered by source, environment, or event name |

Use `defineChannel` for other platforms, such as Discord.

## Handler results

Hooks on the GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and PagerDuty channels, such as
`onPullRequest` or `onIncident`, return one of three results:

| Return value | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `{ auth }` | Runs the model turn with that auth. It can also set the turn's `message`, `title`, or `context` |
| `{ task }` | Runs your function on the host. That function can call `send` to start a model turn |
| `null` | Ignores the event |

## Hosted session keys

On Cursor hosting, each request to a `defineChannel` route starts a new session
unless it carries `X-BDK-Session-Key`. Requests with the same value on one
channel share one session, in arrival order. The handler's
`continuationToken` doesn't change that choice, and local `serve` ignores the
header.

| Rule | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Auth | The alias token or `sharedSecretAuth()`. Routes admitted by `hmacSignatureAuth()` or `publicEndpoint()` answer `400` |
| Value | 1 to 256 printable ASCII characters with no space or comma, or the request gets `400`. Hosting stores the value, so keep secrets and personal data out of it |
| Scope | One channel on one deployment. Prebuilt channels ignore the header |
| Retries | Hosting doesn't deduplicate. A retry runs a second turn |

## Related

- [Webhooks](/docs/guides/webhooks.md)
- [Sessions](/docs/reference/sessions.md)

Source: /docs/reference/cli.md

# Agent SDK CLI

The CLI needs Node 22.13 or newer. Run `agent-sdk <command> --help` to see
every flag for that command.

```text
agent-sdk <command>
```

`agent-sdk help --all` prints every command, and
`agent-sdk help <command> --json` prints one command's flags as JSON.

Commands are named `agent-sdk <resource> <verb>`, such as
`agent-sdk deployment list`, apart from workflow verbs such as `init`, `dev`,
and `deploy`. Older names, such as `agent-sdk deployments` or
`agent-sdk secrets set`, still run and print the new form on stderr. The `bdk`
command remains available.

## Command catalog

### Development commands

| Command | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `help`, `--help`, `-h` | Print the command index, or one command's help |
| [`serve`](#serve) | Serve one or more agents over HTTP |
| [`dev`](#dev) | Serve agents with local-development behavior |
| [`docs`](#docs) | Serve the bundled documentation |
| [`init`](#init) | Scaffold a project, or convert an Automation |
| [`migrate`](#migrate) | Open a pull request that migrates an early-alpha project |
| [`skills list`, `skills install`](#skills-install) | List or refresh the bundled coding-agent skills |
| [`info`](#info) | Print a project's discovered parts or deployment manifest |
| [`validate`](#validate) | Check project diagnostics and set the exit status |
| [`version`](#version) | Print the installed package version |
| [`update`](#update) | Upgrade the installed CLI |
| [`login`, `logout`, `whoami`](#login-logout-whoami) | Store, remove, or show the Cursor credential |

### Session and eval commands

| Command | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| [`chat`](#chat) | Talk to a running agent, or reattach a session |
| [`run`](#run) | Run turns on a local or running agent |
| [`tool call`](#tool-call) | Call a server tool without a model turn |
| [`logs`](#logs) | Follow or dump agent logs |
| [`session list`](#session-list) | List sessions, or their costs |
| [`session get`](#session-get) | Inspect a session or a saved trace |
| [`session create`](#session-create) | Start or continue a hosted session |
| [`eval`](#eval) | Run evals, or list, get, and cancel remote eval batches |

### Managed hosting commands

| Command | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| [`deploy`](#deploy) | Deploy an agent |
| [`deployment list`, `deployment get`](#deployment-list) | List deployments, or inspect one |
| [`deployment stop`, `start`, `kill`, `unlock`, `cancel-runs`, `upgrade`, `rollback`, `delete`, `rotate-token`](#deployment-lifecycle) | Change a deployment's state, release, or alias token |
| [`deployment update`](#deployment-update) | Replace a deployment's event repositories |
| [`secret`](#secret) | Set, list, or delete deployment secrets |

### Connection and channel commands

| Command | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| [`mcp serve`, `mcp install`](#mcp) | Connect an MCP client to an agent |
| [`mcp oauth`](#mcp-oauth) | Authorize an MCP connection |
| [`slack`](#slack) | Provision and check Slack channel apps |
| [`github`](#github) | Forward, replay, and inspect GitHub webhooks |
| [`gitlab`, `bitbucket`, `pagerduty`](#replay-other-webhooks) | Replay and inspect GitLab, Bitbucket, or PagerDuty webhooks |

## Targets {#choose-a-target}

| Target | Selection | Commands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ephemeral local server | Omit `--url` and `--prod` | `run`, `tool call`, `eval` |
| Running server | Pass `--url <baseUrl>` | `chat`, `run`, `tool call`, `eval`, `logs`, `session list`, `session get`, `mcp serve` |
| Default local server | Omit `--url` and `--prod` to use `http://127.0.0.1:3000` | `chat`, `logs`, `session list`, `session get` |
| Hosted deployment | Pass `--prod` | `session list`, `session get`, `logs`. `session create` is always hosted. |

A hosted deployment supports only the commands in its row. `chat`, `run`,
`tool call`, `eval`, `mcp serve`, and `mcp install` exit with a usage error
when you pass `--prod`. To test a hosted agent, start a turn with
[`session create`](#session-create) and inspect it with
[`session get`](#session-get).

`--url` and `--prod` are mutually exclusive. An explicit `--url` must include
the slug for a multi-agent server, such as `http://127.0.0.1:3000/pr-approver`.
Otherwise `--slug` picks the agent, and under `--prod` it defaults to the
`--dir` basename. `--json` prints one JSON document on stdout, including
errors. Without it, output is text, even when piped.

## Local servers

### Serve agents {#serve}

`serve` mounts every project discovered under `--dir`:

```text
agent-sdk serve [--dir <path>] [--port <n>] [--host <host>]
  [--mode multi|single] [--dev] [--api-key <key>]
  [--state-root <path>]
  [--bearer-token <secret> | --allow-anonymous]
  [--allow-anonymous-cursor-github]
  [--allow-anonymous-cursor-account-mcp]
  [--public-url <url>]
  [--peers-url <url>]
  [--no-schedules] [--no-playground] [--no-docs]
  [--cursor-events --repo <owner/name>]...
```

`serve` listens on `127.0.0.1:3000`, or the next free port when that one is
taken. `--mode multi`, the default, mounts each project at `/<slug>/v1/*`, and
`--mode single` mounts one project at `/v1/*`. `--dev` turns off schedule and
reminder firing and admits unsigned loopback GitHub deliveries.

`--bearer-token` requires a token on routes that don't declare their own
authentication. `--allow-anonymous` admits every caller as one principal, so
use it only behind a trusted network boundary. The slugs `v1`, `playground`,
and `docs` are reserved.

### Develop locally {#dev}

`dev` is `serve --dev` with an optional project path:

```text
agent-sdk dev
agent-sdk dev ./agent-sdk-pr-reviewer --port 3000
```

It accepts every `serve` option. Don't combine the path with a different
`--dir`.

### Serve the docs {#docs}

```text
agent-sdk docs [--port <n>] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--print]
```

`docs` serves the bundled documentation on a loopback port until you press
Ctrl-C. `--print` prints the URL without opening a browser.

## Sessions and turns

### Chat with an agent {#chat}

```text
agent-sdk chat [--url <baseUrl>] [--message <text>]
  [--session <id> | --resume] [--continuation-token <token>]
  [--slug <slug>] [--json] [--text] [--no-color]
```

On a TTY, `chat` opens a REPL and sends any `--message` first. Without a TTY, it
sends `--message` as one turn, or reads newline-delimited messages until EOF.
`--session <id>` reattaches a stored session, and `--resume` picks the most
recent one.

### Run turns {#run}

```text
agent-sdk run [--dir <path>] [--message <text>]...
  [--messages-file <path>] [--url <baseUrl>]
  [--session <id>] [--continuation-token <token>]
  [--trace <file> | --no-trace] [--json]
  [--timeout-ms <n>] [--no-stream] [--slug <slug>] [--dry-run]
```

Repeat `--message` for a multi-turn run. `run` prints the compact trajectory,
writes an NDJSON trace unless you pass `--no-trace`, and exits `1` when the
trajectory fails. It has no default timeout.

### Call a tool {#tool-call}

```text
agent-sdk tool call <tool> [--input <json>]
  [--dir <path> | --url <baseUrl>]
  [--session <id>] [--slug <slug>] [--json]
```

`--input` takes JSON and defaults to `{}`. `--session` runs the tool in that
session's workspace and records the call. The command exits `1` unless the
response has `ok: true`. See
[Tools](/docs/reference/tools.md#call-a-tool-without-a-model-turn) for error codes.

### List sessions {#session-list}

```text
agent-sdk session list [--url <baseUrl> | --prod] [--since <duration|instant>]
  [--view sessions|cost] [--slug <slug>] [--team <id>]
  [--bearer-token <token>] [--limit <n>] [--page-token <token>] [--json]
```

`--limit` sets the page size, 20 by default and at most 100. With `--prod`,
it lists the most recently active hosted sessions, and `--since` reads back
to a cutoff such as `24h` or an ISO-8601 instant.
`--view cost` works only against a running server.

### Inspect a session {#session-get}

```text
agent-sdk session get <sessionId> [--url <baseUrl> | --prod]
  [--slug <slug>] [--team <id>]
  [--view trajectory|events|cost] [--json [--fields <a,b.c>]]
  [--trace <file.ndjson>] [--web [--print]]

agent-sdk session get --file <file.ndjson> [--json]
```

`session get` prints a compact trajectory, or raw [events](/docs/reference/sessions.md#stream-events) with `--view events`. `--view cost` and `--trace` work only locally. `--file` reads a saved trace and exits `1` when that trajectory failed, and `--web` opens the session in the playground. For a hosted deployment:

```bash
agent-sdk session list --prod
agent-sdk session get <sessionId> --prod --slug <slug> --view events
```

### Start a hosted session {#session-create}

```text
agent-sdk session create --message <text> [--session <ses_...>]
  [--slug <slug>] [--team <id>] [--wait [--timeout-ms <n>]]
  [--read-only] [--as-of <instant>] [--component <key>] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

`session create` sends one `--message` to the hosted deployment. Without
`--wait`, it exits `0` once the deployment accepts the turn, before a new
session has an ID. `--wait` polls until the session starts. It exits `3` when
`--timeout-ms` passes first and `1` when the delivery is skipped or fails.

`--session` continues a session that `session create` started. `--read-only`
stubs write tools, and `--as-of` freezes the session's clock at an ISO-8601
instant. See [Verify a hosted turn](/docs/deployment.md#verify-a-hosted-turn).

### Follow logs {#logs}

```text
agent-sdk logs [sessionId] [--url <baseUrl> | --prod]
  [--session <sessionId>] [--slug <slug>] [--team <id>] [--once] [--json]
```

`logs` follows output until Ctrl-C, and `--once` prints the current buffer and
exits. With `--prod`, it follows the hosted deployment's recent sessions and
prints a `==> <sessionId> (<channel>) <==` header when the output switches
sessions. A session ID follows one hosted session and requires `--prod`.

## Evals

### Run evals {#eval}

`eval` discovers `evals/**/*.eval.{ts,js}` and runs the selected cases:

```text
agent-sdk eval [--dir <path>] [evalId...]
  [--list] [--tag <tag>]... [--json] [--verbose]
  [--timeout-ms <n>] [--strict] [--max-concurrency <n>]
  [--junit <path>] [--artifacts <dir> | --no-artifacts]
  [--skip-report] [--no-stream]
  [--url <baseUrl>] [--no-wait] [--slug <slug>]
```

Select an exact case such as `weather/nyc`, a file prefix such as `weather`,
several IDs, or none for every case. Put an ID that is also a subcommand word
after `--`, as in `agent-sdk eval -- list`. The project needs an
[eval configuration](/docs/reference/evals.md#eval-configuration).

`--strict` fails a scored case below its soft threshold. The command exits `1`
for failed cases and `2` for invalid options or no matching cases. A running
server prints an Eval ID when it accepts the batch, and `--no-wait` returns at
that point. These commands require `--url`:

```text
agent-sdk eval list --url <baseUrl> [--limit <n>] [--page-token <token>]
agent-sdk eval get <evalId> --url <baseUrl>
agent-sdk eval cancel <evalId> --url <baseUrl>
```

`eval get` exits `3` while the batch runs and `1` when it failed or was
cancelled.

## Projects

### Scaffold a project {#init}

```text
agent-sdk init [directory] [--template <name>] [--var id=value]... [--json] [--dry-run]
agent-sdk init [directory] --from automation:<url-or-uuid> [--dry-run] [--json]
```

Without a directory, `init` prints the setup guide. With one, it adds missing
scaffold files, installs dependencies, and tries to put `agent-sdk` on `PATH`.
On a TTY, it also asks the template's questions and starts login when needed.

`--template` takes `agentic-owners`, `agents-md`, `code-wiki`, `demo`,
`security-help`, `security-reviewer`, `thermo-quality-review`, `thermo-review`,
`triage-jira`, or `triage-linear`. `triage` selects `triage-linear`.
`--var id=value` answers a template question without a prompt. `--dry-run`
lists the files without writing them.

#### Convert an Automation {#convert-automation}

`--from automation:` takes a Cursor Automation dashboard URL or UUID and
writes to `./<automation-name>` unless you name a directory. Generated files
don't overwrite existing paths, but the `npm install` that follows can run
lifecycle scripts from an existing `package.json`. See
[Convert a Cursor Automation](/docs/guides/convert-automation.md).

### Migrate an early-alpha project {#migrate}

```text
agent-sdk migrate [--dir <path>] [--repo <https-url>] [--ref <git-ref>]
  [--path <agent-path>] [--no-wait] [--json] [--api-key <key>]
```

`migrate` applies only to projects that deployed with `architecture: "v1"`
during the early alpha. It starts a Cursor cloud agent on a pushed Git ref
with the bundled `bdk-migrate-v2` skill, and the agent opens a pull request
with the source changes. The command never deploys or changes secrets.

With nothing to change, it prints `Nothing to migrate.` and exits `0`, and it exits `1` if the run ends without a pull request. `deploy` refuses a project that sets `architecture: "v1"` and points to `migrate`. See [Migrate an early-alpha project](/docs/guides/migrate.md).

### Install and list coding-agent skills {#skills-install}

```text
agent-sdk skills install [--dry-run] [--json]
agent-sdk skills list [--json [--fields <a,b.c>]] [--limit <n>] [--page-token <token>]
```

Package installation copies the bundled skills, `skills install` replaces the installed copies and removes stale ones, and `skills list` prints each skill's bundled and installed versions. The `bdk-cli` skill teaches agents to run `agent-sdk` safely.

### Inspect a project {#info}

```text
agent-sdk info [--dir <path>] [--view info|manifest] [--json [--fields <a,b.c>]]
```

Text output lists what discovery found, such as tools, channels, and
diagnostics. `--view manifest` summarizes one project's deployment metadata
without a network request.

### Validate a project {#validate}

```text
agent-sdk validate [--dir <path>]
```

`validate` prints every discovered project's diagnostics and exits `1` when
any diagnostic has error severity. `validate` fails when an SCM webhook secret
or GitHub credential is a literal or a getter, and the error message shows the
`{ secretName }` form to use. A project that still sets `architecture: "v1"`
gets the same finding as a warning.

## Credentials and versions

### Manage credentials {#login-logout-whoami}

```text
agent-sdk login [--api-key <key>] [--key-name <name>]
agent-sdk whoami [--json]
agent-sdk logout
```

`login` stores a supplied API key, or opens browser sign-in and stores the key
it creates. `whoami` shows the active credential and its source. `logout`
removes the stored credential but doesn't revoke the key, so revoke it in the
Cursor dashboard.

### Print the version {#version}

```text
agent-sdk version [--json]
agent-sdk --version
```

### Update the CLI {#update}

```text
agent-sdk update
```

`update` upgrades a recognized global or project install to npm's `latest`
tag, or prints a manual upgrade command. Published installs check for updates
daily unless an [update-check variable](#environment-variables) is set.

## Managed hosting

Every command here that changes a deployment takes `--dry-run`, which runs
the reads, stops at the first change, prints that request with secrets
redacted, and exits `0`.

`secret delete`, `image delete`, `slack destroy`, and the `deployment`
commands marked No in the [lifecycle table](#deployment-lifecycle) can't be
undone. On a terminal they ask you to type the slug or name, and a mismatch
exits `1`. Without a terminal, they exit `2` unless you pass `--yes`.

### Deploy agents {#deploy}

```text
agent-sdk deploy [--dir <path>] [--slug <slug> | --all] [--team <id>]
  [--repo <https-url>] [--ref <git-ref>] [--path <agent-path>]
  [--cursor-events-repo <repo>]... [--no-wait] [--json]
```

Deploying needs a team with agent hosting turned on, and a team service-account key with agent access can deploy. The CLI infers `--repo`, `--ref`, and `--path` from the current checkout, and the repository must use HTTPS.

`deploy` deploys one agent. On a folder of several agents, pass `--slug` to
pick one. `--all`, or picking several agents, prints one
`agent-sdk deploy --dir` command per agent and exits `1`.

`--cursor-events-repo` sets the repositories whose Cursor events the
deployment receives. Write `owner/name` for GitHub,
`gitlab.com/<group>/<project>` for GitLab, or
`bitbucket.org/<workspace>/<repo>` for Bitbucket. A GitLab path can include
subgroups. Repeat the flag once per repository. Each deploy replaces the whole list. Without the flag, the deployment watches its GitHub
source repository.

`deploy` waits until the deployment runs and exits nonzero if it fails, unless
you pass `--no-wait`. The first deploy of a slug can print an alias token
once. Slugs use lowercase letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, start with a letter
or digit, and have at most 64 characters. See [Deployment](/docs/deployment.md)
for egress hosts and the alias token.

### Inspect deployments {#deployment-list}

```text
agent-sdk deployment list [--team <id>] [--limit <n>] [--page-token <token>]
  [--json [--fields <a,b.c>]]
agent-sdk deployment get <slug> [--team <id>] [--json [--fields <a,b.c>]] [--web]
```

`deployment list` shows each deployment's slug, status, and update time, and `deployment get` adds the release, watched repositories, routes, secret names, and latest error. `--web` opens the deployment in [Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents), and an early-alpha deployment shows the steps to migrate it.

### Change a deployment {#deployment-lifecycle}

```text
agent-sdk deployment <command> <slug> [--team <id>] [--json] [--dry-run]
```

| Command | What it does | Undoable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stop` | Stop the deployment. `--cancel-runs` also cancels active runs and reminder wakes. | Yes |
| `start` | Resume a stopped deployment. A kill lock stays. | Yes |
| `kill` | Lock deploys, stop the deployment, and cancel its runs and reminder wakes. To recover, run `unlock` and then `start`. | No |
| `unlock` | Remove the kill lock so deploys, upgrades, and rollbacks work again. Traffic stays stopped. | Yes |
| `cancel-runs` | Cancel active runs and reminder wakes. | No |
| `update` | Replace the [event repositories](#deployment-update). | Yes |
| `upgrade` | Move to a ready release, the newest unless you pass `--release`. | Yes |
| `rollback` | Move to an earlier ready release, the previous one unless you pass `--release`. | Yes |
| `delete` | Remove the deployment and free its slug. | No |
| `rotate-token` | Replace the alias token. The old one stops working at once. | No |

### Replace event repositories {#deployment-update}

```text
agent-sdk deployment update <slug> (--event-repo <owner/name>... | --no-event-repos)
  [--team <id>] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

The repositories you pass replace the deployment's whole event repository
list, and `--no-event-repos` clears it.

### Manage deployment secrets {#secret}

```text
agent-sdk secret set <slug> NAME [NAME2 ...]
  [--team <id>] [--from-argv] [--json]
agent-sdk secret list <slug> [--team <id>] [--limit <n>] [--page-token <token>] [--json]
agent-sdk secret delete <slug> NAME [--team <id>] [--yes] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

On a TTY, `secret set` prompts for each hidden value. With one name,
redirected stdin is the whole value minus one trailing newline, so a PEM key
keeps its line breaks:

```bash
agent-sdk secret set my-bot GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY < ./app.private-key.pem
```

With several names, give one line per name. `set` rejects `NAME=VALUE` arguments unless you pass `--from-argv`, because shell history keeps them. Names use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, and the `CURSOR_` prefix is reserved. `secret list` returns names, never values.

## MCP connections

### Connect an MCP client {#mcp}

```text
agent-sdk mcp serve --url <baseUrl> [--bearer-token <token>]

agent-sdk mcp install --url <baseUrl> [--bearer-token <token>]
  [--name <server-name>] [--dry-run] [--json]
```

`mcp serve` proxies newline-delimited JSON-RPC from stdin to the agent's MCP
endpoint and reserves stdout for MCP messages. `mcp install` adds the agent to
`~/.cursor/mcp.json`. An entry made with `--bearer-token` contains that token,
so treat every printed or written copy as a credential.

### Authorize MCP OAuth {#mcp-oauth}

```text
agent-sdk mcp oauth <connection> [--dir <path>]
  [--slug <slug>] [--team <id>]
```

`<connection>` is the basename under `bot/mcp-connections/` or
`bot/host-connections/`. A `url` connection with `oauth: true` opens a browser
PKCE flow and saves tokens bound to that URL, so authorize again after you
change it. A `cursorAccount` connection exits nonzero and points to the
cursor.com dashboard. See [Host MCP OAuth](/docs/guides/mcp-oauth.md).

## Channel helpers

### Configure Slack {#slack}

```text
agent-sdk slack setup
agent-sdk slack create [--dir <path>] [--name <name>] [--env prod]
  [--slack-team <id>] [--team <id>] [--icon <url-or-file>]
  [--prefix <prefix> | --no-prefix] [--channel-posts] [--json]
agent-sdk slack destroy [--dir <path>] [--env prod] [--yes] [--dry-run]
  [--slack-team <id>] [--team <id>] [--json]
agent-sdk slack icon <url-or-file> [--dir <path>] [--env prod]
  [--slack-team <id>] [--team <id>] [--json]
agent-sdk slack init --manual [--dir <path>] [--name <name>]
  [--prefix <prefix> | --no-prefix] [--channel-posts]
  [--install | --no-install] [--slack-team <id>] [--env dev|prod]
agent-sdk slack manifest [--dir <path>] [--name <name>]
  [--env dev|prod|both] [--channel-posts] [--dry-run]
agent-sdk slack doctor [--dir <path>]
  [--prefix <prefix> | --no-prefix] [--channel <id>]... [--json]
```

`slack create` opens the
[Deployed Agents](https://cursor.com/dashboard/deployed-agents) wizard, writes
the token pair to `.env.local`, and runs `doctor`, which checks both tokens and
Socket Mode. It makes the development app unless you pass `--env prod`. The
token prefix defaults to the project directory name in upper snake case.
`--channel-posts` adds the message events that `engagement.channelPosts`
needs. See [Slack](/docs/guides/slack.md) for manual setup.

### Test GitHub webhooks {#github}

```text
agent-sdk github forward [--dir <path>] [--slug <slug>] [--channel <id>]
  [--repo owner/repo | --org <org>] [--events a,b,c]
  [--url <url>] [--host <host>] [--port <n>]
  [--secret <secret>] [--install]
agent-sdk github replay <pr-url-or-owner/repo#N>
  [--events a,b,c | '*'] [--action <action>] [--conclusion <result>]
  [--comment <body>] [--context <name>] [--dir <path>]
  [--slug <slug>] [--channel <id>] [--url <url>]
  [--secret <secret>] [--dry-run] [--fixtures-dir <dir>] [--json]
agent-sdk github events [--dir <path>] [--host <host>] [--port <n>] [--json]
agent-sdk github doctor [--install] [--json]
```

`forward` sends live deliveries to discovered channels through `gh webhook forward`. It needs repository admin access, or organization owner access for `--org`, and it uses the GitHub CLI's own login, so unset `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `GH_TOKEN` first. `doctor` checks the GitHub CLI and its webhook extension.

`replay` reads a pull request with read access, builds webhook payloads, and
posts them to matching channels. Its events are `pull_request`, the default,
`issue_comment`, `pull_request_review_comment`, `check_run`, `check_suite`,
`workflow_run`, and `status`. `--dry-run` prints the payloads without posting,
and `--fixtures-dir` also writes them as fixtures. See
[GitHub](/docs/guides/github.md) for channel setup.

### Test GitLab, Bitbucket, and PagerDuty webhooks {#replay-other-webhooks}

```text
agent-sdk gitlab replay <mr-url-or-group/project!N> [replay flags]
agent-sdk bitbucket replay <pr-url-or-workspace/repo#N> [replay flags]
agent-sdk pagerduty replay [incident-id] [replay flags]
agent-sdk <gitlab|bitbucket|pagerduty> events [--dir <path>] [--json]
agent-sdk <gitlab|bitbucket> forward [--dir <path>]
```

Replay takes the same flags as `github replay`, including `--fixtures-dir`. `events` lists the discovered channels, and `forward` prints the webhook and tunnel recipe for live deliveries.

| Command | Replay events | Default event | Read credential | `--secret` default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gitlab replay` | `merge_request`, `note`, `pipeline`, `push` | `merge_request` | `GITLAB_TOKEN` | `GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| `bitbucket replay` | `pullrequest:created`, `pullrequest:updated`, `pullrequest:comment_created`, `repo:push`, in Cloud or Data Center format | `pullrequest:created` | `BITBUCKET_TOKEN` | `BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| `pagerduty replay` | `incident.triggered`, `.acknowledged`, `.annotated`, `.escalated`, `.resolved`, `.reopened` | `incident.triggered` | None | `PAGERDUTY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` |

PagerDuty replay's incident ID defaults to `PREPLAY1`, and `--comment` is the
note body for `annotated`. Without a secret, its deliveries are unsigned, and
`agent-sdk dev` admits them from loopback. See [GitLab](/docs/guides/gitlab.md),
[Bitbucket](/docs/guides/bitbucket.md), and [PagerDuty](/docs/guides/pagerduty.md)
for channel setup.

## Environment variables {#environment-variables}

The CLI tries `--api-key`, `CURSOR_API_KEY`, `CURSOR_API_KEY_FILE`,
`CURSOR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY`, then the stored `agent-sdk login` credential, in
that order.

| Variable | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `CURSOR_API_KEY` | Cursor credential. |
| `CURSOR_API_KEY_FILE` | Path to a Cursor credential file. |
| `CURSOR_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY` | Team service-account credential. |
| `CURSOR_API_BASE_URL` | Backend for login, account, deployment, and event commands. |
| `CURSOR_BACKEND_URL` | Backend for agent turns. Set it with `CURSOR_API_BASE_URL` for a non-default backend. |
| `AGENT_SERVE_CONFIG_DIR` | CLI config directory for stored credentials and update state. |
| `AGENT_SERVE_NO_UPDATE_CHECK`, `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER`, `CI` | Turn off update checks when set to a value other than `0`. |
| `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Default secret for GitHub forwarding and replay. |
| `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, `GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID` | GitHub App credentials for outbound API calls. |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN` | Tokens for outbound GitHub calls. |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | GitLab API token and default webhook token. |
| `GITLAB_API_BASE_URL` | GitLab REST base URL for self-managed hosts. |
| `BITBUCKET_TOKEN`, `BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Bitbucket API token and default signing secret. |
| `BITBUCKET_API_BASE_URL` | Bitbucket Data Center REST base URL. |
| `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`, `SLACK_APP_TOKEN` | Slack tokens for one agent. Multi-agent servers use `<PREFIX>_SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` and `<PREFIX>_SLACK_APP_TOKEN`. |

## Exit status

Every command uses these exit codes, and `agent-sdk help --json` lists them
as `exitCodes`.

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | `ok` |
| `1` | `failed`, `aborted`, `invalid_argument`, `rate_limited`, or `unavailable` |
| `2` | `usage`, for a bad command, flag, or argument |
| `3` | `pending`, while the work still runs |
| `4` | `not_found` |
| `5` | `unauthenticated` or `permission_denied` |
| `6` | `conflict` or `failed_precondition` |

- [Deployment](/docs/deployment.md)
